blocks.heading: Clear information. Honest limits. No promotion.
blocks.body:
Every person considering breast enhancement has different anatomy, health needs, preferences and expectations. This website is an educational resource, not a clinic, and it cannot recommend a treatment for any individual. Its purpose is to help you understand the choices before discussing them with a qualified clinician.

We explain what each option is intended to do and distinguish procedures designed to change breast volume from those that may affect appearance in other ways. A treatment being described as “non-surgical” does not necessarily mean it is effective, risk-free or suitable for breast enlargement.

Our guides draw on published research and guidance from health authorities and professional organisations. Where possible, we link to original sources and explain the strength and limitations of the evidence. When evidence is uncertain, limited or does not support a claim, we aim to say so clearly.

For each approach, we consider potential benefits alongside limitations, recovery, alternatives and safety questions. The goal is to support realistic expectations and better-prepared conversations with a qualified healthcare professional—not to rush or promote a decision.

blocks.title: An important clinical distinction
blocks.text: Injectable fillers, threads, PRP and biostimulators should not be presented as interchangeable alternatives to breast augmentation surgery. Their evidence, indications and ability to increase breast volume differ substantially, and a procedure being described as “non-surgical” does not by itself make it safe.

blocks.heading: A clear, five-step pathway to an informed decision
blocks.lead: Use these steps to move from exploring options to preparing informed questions. Take your time; a decision about your body should never be rushed by advertising.

items.title: Learn what each option is
items.text: Start with the surgical and non-surgical guides. Check what a treatment is intended to do, how it is performed and what it cannot reliably achieve.

items.title: Check what the evidence shows
items.text: Use the evidence guide and linked research sources to distinguish established findings from limited, emerging or unsupported claims. Look at the source and its limitations, not just a headline or advertisement.

items.title: Understand suitability and safety
items.text: Review candidacy, contraindications, possible complications, recovery and warning signs. Suitability depends on your health and circumstances and needs an individual clinical assessment.

items.title: Compare options fairly
items.text: Compare the intended effect, evidence, likely limitations, recovery, risks, alternatives and potential need for future care. Consider whether an option matches your goals—not only its advertised benefits.

items.title: Prepare questions for a clinician
items.text: Write down what matters to you and discuss it with a registered, appropriately qualified healthcare professional. Ask about their credentials, the exact product or technique, realistic outcomes, alternatives, costs, aftercare and how complications are managed. Take time to consider the answers and seek another opinion if you need one.

blocks.heading: A personal decision that needs careful planning
blocks.body:
Breast augmentation is a surgical option for increasing breast volume or changing breast shape. It may involve implants or, for selected people, their own fat.

People may consider it for greater fullness, a change in proportions, or restoration of volume after pregnancy or weight change.

What guides the plan

An assessment should consider anatomy, existing breast tissue, skin characteristics, general health, lifestyle, expectations, willingness to accept surgical risks and the need for future follow-up. An appropriately credentialed surgeon should lead this assessment.

blocks.html:
Breast augmentation: data from the American Society of Plastic Surgeons

The figures and lists below summarise patient information published by the American Society of Plastic Surgeons (ASPS), the largest association of board-certified plastic surgeons in the United States. They are reproduced here for education and context. ASPS guidance reflects United States practice and regulation and does not replace assessment by a suitably qualified clinician in your own jurisdiction.

blocks.heading: What breast augmentation can — and cannot — do
head: Goal
What ASPS patient information says
rows: Breast implants or fat transfer can increase the size and projection of the breasts.
Augmentation can improve the balance between breast and hip contours.
ASPS notes the procedure may enhance self-image and self-confidence.
Implants may also be used for breast reconstruction after mastectomy or injury.
Augmentation alone does not correct severely drooping breasts; a breast lift may be needed, at the same time or as a separate operation.

blocks.heading: Implants, fat transfer and injectable options
blocks.lead: The four approaches shown here add volume in different ways — and differ in evidence, duration and risk.

blocks.caption: AI-generated conceptual illustration. Not a real patient or a prediction of treatment results.

blocks.heading: How the procedure is usually performed
blocks.lead: ASPS describes the operation in five broad stages.

items.title: Anesthesia
items.text: Intravenous sedation or general anaesthesia is used, so the procedure is comfortable throughout.

items.title: Incision
items.text: Peri-areolar, inframammary fold or axillary incisions are the usual routes; ASPS notes that the belly-button approach carries a higher complication rate.

items.title: Placement
items.text: The implant is placed either under the pectoral muscle (submuscular) or behind the breast tissue over the muscle (subglandular).

items.title: Closure
items.text: Layered sutures close the tissue, with sutures, skin adhesive or surgical tape on the skin. Scars fade over time and are affected by genetics, nicotine and infection.

items.title: Results
items.text: Results are visible immediately, with the final shape settling as swelling resolves.

blocks.heading: Types of breast implants
head: Implant
What ASPS patient information says
rows: Sterile salt water; collapses and is absorbed or expelled if the shell leaks; uniform shape and firmness; FDA-approved from age 18.
Salt water with an internal structure for a more natural feel.
Gel feels more like natural breast tissue; does not collapse if it leaks; regular ultrasound or MRI screening is advised; FDA-approved from age 22.
Keeps its shape even if the shell breaks; firmer and thicker; a shaped version gives more bottom projection but can look unusual if it rotates; requires a longer incision.
Generally a fuller look; higher profiles add more projection; less concern about rotation.
Softest feel and natural movement, but rippling may be felt or seen.
Tissue adheres to the surface so it is less likely to move and may reduce capsular contracture, but textured surfaces are where BIA-ALCL occurs most often.

blocks.title: Recovery and results (ASPS patient information)
blocks.text:
• Immediately after surgery the breasts are wrapped in gauze, with an elastic bandage or support bra to limit swelling and support healing.
  • Patients are monitored in recovery and are usually permitted home about an hour after surgery once stable for discharge.
  • The support garment (a bra or elastic band) is worn around the clock as instructed; wound care instructions differ between surgeons and should be followed exactly.
  • Acute pain typically subsides after one to five days, but soreness and swelling may persist for a few weeks.
  • Final results settle over a few weeks as swelling subsides; incision lines may take several months to a couple of years to fade.
  • Breasts change over time with ageing, weight fluctuation, hormones and gravity; some people later choose a lift or an implant exchange.
  • Implants are not guaranteed to last a lifetime, so further surgery may eventually be needed.

blocks.title: Risks and safety (ASPS patient information)
blocks.text:
ASPS lists the following possible risks of breast augmentation surgery, discussed fully before consent:

  • Anaesthesia risks.
  • Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL) or other very rare cancers in the capsule, such as breast implant-associated squamous cell carcinoma (BIA-SCC).
  • Bleeding or haematoma.
  • Changes in nipple or breast sensation.
  • Fluid accumulation (seroma).
  • Tight scar tissue forming around the implant (capsular contracture).
  • Implant leakage or rupture.
  • Infection and persistent pain.
  • Poor scarring, wrinkling of the skin over the implant, or the implant sitting in the wrong position.
  • The possibility that revision surgery will be needed.

For silicone implants, the FDA recommends screening with MRI or ultrasound five to six years after placement and every two to three years thereafter. Risk factors include pregnancy, weight change and the menopause. Routine examinations help confirm that an implant is intact, because a ruptured implant sometimes causes no symptoms.

blocks.heading: US average costs
head: Procedure

blocks.heading: Incision sites, scar healing and aftercare

blocks.html:
Scars are an expected part of breast augmentation surgery, and where they sit is governed mainly by the incision used to create the implant pocket. Their final appearance depends on incision choice, skin type, genetics, tension on the wound and aftercare. The sections below describe the usual incision options, how scars typically mature and which general measures support healing. Outcomes, risks and suitability vary between individuals, and an in-person medical assessment is required before any treatment decision.

Incision options and where scars sit

Surgeons reach the breast and the implant pocket through a small number of standard routes. The choice balances surgical access, the implant type and implant placement, the surgeon's training, and the patient's anatomy and preferences. Incisions are usually planned so that resulting lines fall within natural skin folds or along the border between skin and areolar pigment, where they are simpler to conceal in ordinary clothing. No incision leaves skin without a mark; planning aims to keep lines discreet rather than absent.

Inframammary fold

The inframammary incision sits in the crease beneath the breast. It provides direct access to the pocket and is used for both silicone and saline devices, as well as for many revision procedures. The line is hidden within the fold when standing, although its visibility changes with posture and clothing. Where the fold is shallow, or where the two sides differ, the surgeon plans the crease position carefully so the scar does not sit too high or too low. Heavier or larger breast implant sizes can place more tension on this line during healing.

Periareolar

A periareolar incision follows the lower border of the areola, where darker and lighter pigment meet. It can be a reasonable option where that border is well defined. The route passes through breast tissue, and surgeons discuss possible implications for nipple sensation and breastfeeding in general terms at consultation. Scar visibility depends on how the line heals along the pigment boundary, and this varies with skin type and individual tendency to pigmentation change.

Transaxillary

A transaxillary incision is placed within the armpit crease, so no scar appears on the breast skin itself. It is used with particular implant types and operative approaches and depends on the surgeon's training and the patient's anatomy. Because the working distance to the breast is longer, later surgery is not always possible through the same route, and some revisions require an additional incision. Consultation therefore covers these limitations alongside the position of the scar.

Comparing the three approaches

ApproachTypical scar positionPoints in favourPoints to discuss
Inframammary foldCrease beneath the breastDirect access; commonly used for primary and revision surgeryLine may be visible in some positions; fold position needs planning
PeriareolarLower border of the areolaPigment boundary can soften the linePasses through breast tissue; healing varies by skin type
TransaxillaryArmpit creaseNo scar on the breast skinTechnique dependent; later access can be limited

How scars mature over time

Scar healing is usually described in overlapping phases rather than fixed stages. In the first weeks the line is commonly pink or red, slightly raised and firm to touch, and itching or tightness is frequent. Over the following months collagen remodels, and the scar typically becomes flatter, softer and paler. Maturation frequently continues for a year or longer, and some lines keep changing beyond that. These descriptions are indicative only; the pace and the final appearance vary widely between individuals.

Skin type and genetics influence the result. Darker skin tones may be more prone to pigmentation change, and some people form raised or keloid scarring whatever the incision used. The skin of the breast also carries tension, particularly with heavier devices, which can widen a line over many months. Terms such as hypertrophic and keloid scarring are explained in the site glossary, which may help when reading clinical letters.

Patients often ask what they will see at each stage. In the early weeks the line may look prominent and feel tight; by the third month it is commonly flatter though still coloured; through the second half of the first year it usually continues to soften. Some people find the scar most noticeable at three to six months and quieter afterwards, while for others change is slow and steady. Clinical photographs taken at follow-up help track progress objectively once memory of the earlier appearance has faded.

General scar care measures

Most surgical teams provide written aftercare instructions, and protocols differ between clinics and between patients. Measures commonly discussed include the following, introduced at the stage of healing your surgeon advises.

  • Protect maturing scars from sunlight. Ultraviolet exposure can darken early scar tissue, so covering the area or using sun protection is commonly advised for several months.
  • Consider silicone gel or sheeting once external healing is complete, following the clinic's instructions on duration and application.
  • Keep incisions clean and dry as directed, and avoid soaking, swimming or heavy sweating until the team confirms it is appropriate.
  • Avoid nicotine completely during healing, because it restricts blood supply to skin and is associated with wound problems.
  • Wear recommended support garments and avoid strain on the incision during the early recovery period.
  • Attend scheduled follow-up so that healing can be assessed and concerns raised early rather than late.

Massage of mature incision lines is advised by some surgical teams and not others, so it should begin only when wounds are confirmed closed and comfortable. Firm pressure over unhealed skin, early underwire bras and adhesive products used too soon can irritate a healing line. If dressings or tapes are used, instructions on when to change or remove them should be followed exactly, and any skin reaction should be reported.

What can make scars less favourable

Several factors can work against neat healing, and many of them are modifiable before and after surgery.

  • Nicotine use of any kind around the time of surgery and throughout healing.
  • Wound tension from heavier implants, early heavy lifting or vigorous upper-body activity.
  • Infection or wound breakdown, which makes widening or distortion of a scar more likely.
  • A personal or family tendency to hypertrophic or keloid scarring.
  • Poor nutrition, poorly controlled chronic conditions, or medicines that affect healing or bleeding.
  • Sun exposure on immature scars, and delayed presentation of wound problems.

These points sit alongside the general breast augmentation risks discussed during consent, and they are reviewed before surgery so that planning reflects individual circumstances.

Scars after fat transfer

Fat transfer breast augmentation avoids implant incisions on the breast in many cases, but small scars remain. Fat is harvested through liposuction access points, commonly on the abdomen, flanks or thighs, and these puncture marks mature like other scars. The marks are usually short, although their number and position depend on the areas treated. Donor areas can also change in contour, and access points may be visible on the skin of the breast where fat is injected. Sun protection, garment use and adherence to aftercare advice apply to donor sites as well as to the breast.

Asymmetry, wide scars and revision scarring

Small differences in scar position, length or width between the two sides are common and often settle as healing progresses. Lines may widen when tension is high, and some patients notice a scar more in certain positions than under clothing. Scar position can also shift slightly as swelling settles and the implant settles into its pocket, so a concern raised at two weeks is assessed differently from one raised at twelve months. Where a scar matures unfavourably, options such as silicone therapy, injections, laser treatment or surgical scar revision can be discussed; these are individualised and are usually considered after maturation is complete. Further breast surgery may reuse an existing line or require a new one, as outlined in breast implant revision. No revision can be promised to produce a particular scar appearance.

When to seek a review

Contact the surgical team promptly if a scar or wound shows spreading redness, increasing warmth or pain, discharge, bleeding, opening of the wound, fever, or a rapidly thickening or painful raised scar. Sudden change in breast shape, a firm painful breast, or a scar that concerns you also warrants review, as does any worry that arises between scheduled visits. Early assessment is preferable to waiting when something feels wrong, and follow-up forms part of the pathway described in breast augmentation surgery patient information.

Scars at your consultation

Useful questions include where scars would sit for your anatomy, which incision suits the planned implant and pocket, how the fold or areolar border is planned, what aftercare is provided, how follow-up is arranged, and how scars are managed if healing is slow. Marketing language implying that surgery can leave skin without marks should be treated with scepticism. This information is educational and is not a substitute for personal medical advice from a qualified clinician.

items.q: Do breast augmentation scars disappear completely?
items.a: Scars do not disappear entirely. They usually soften, flatten and pale over many months to more than a year, but final appearance varies with skin type, genetics, incision site and healing conditions. Surgeons aim to place incisions where lines can be concealed rather than erased.

items.q: Which incision leaves the least noticeable scar?
items.a: Noticeability depends on skin type, healing, clothing and individual preference rather than a single ranking of approaches. Inframammary, periareolar and transaxillary incisions each sit in different anatomical areas with different trade-offs. Suitability is assessed during an in-person consultation.

items.q: How long do breast augmentation scars take to mature?
items.a: Early scars are often pink, raised or firm for the first weeks to months, then gradually flatten and fade. Maturation commonly continues for a year or longer, and the timeline varies between individuals. Follow-up review helps track healing.

items.q: What can make scars worse after breast augmentation?
items.a: Nicotine use, wound tension, infection, poor nutrition and delayed healing can all affect scar quality, and sun exposure can darken immature scars. Following post-operative instructions and attending follow-up supports healing. Individual variation remains important.

items.q: How long does recovery take?
items.a: Recovery varies according to the procedure, surgical technique, individual healing and the clinician’s advice. Your surgeon will give you a personalised return-to-activity timeline.

items.q: Are the results permanent?
items.a: No procedure can promise permanent results. Breast implants are not lifetime devices: additional operations may be needed and complications can occur. Fat transfer results depend on how much transferred fat survives.

pages.h1: Breast Implants: Types, Placement & Long-Term Reality
pages.seoTitle: Breast Implants: Types, Placement & Long-Term Reality | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: An evidence-aware guide to breast implants — saline and silicone, smooth and textured, shape and profile, placement and incisions, longevity, monitoring and the difference from injectable silicone.
pages.bannerLead: Breast implants are medical devices placed surgically to increase breast volume. They are the most studied enlargement method — with real complication and revision rates that every patient should understand before deciding.

breadcrumb.label: Breast Implants: Types, Placement & Long-Term Reality

schema.name: Breast Implants: Types, Placement & Long-Term Reality

blocks.title: Not the same as injectable silicone
blocks.text: Injectable silicone is a different product from a silicone gel-filled implant and must never be used as a substitute. Injectable silicone used to enlarge the breasts can cause serious, potentially permanent harm.

blocks.html: An implant is a device — a shell filled with saline (sterile salt water) or silicone gel — placed behind the breast tissue or behind the pectoral muscle. Implant surgery is the best-documented route to a larger, predictable breast size, but it is surgery: it carries risks, it is not permanent, and follow-up over the years is part of the decision.

blocks.heading: Filling, surface and shape
head: Choice
Options
Trade-offs to understand
rows: Silicone gel tends to feel more like natural breast tissue and does not collapse if it leaks; it requires monitoring for silent rupture. Saline collapses and is absorbed if the shell leaks. Regulators approve saline from age 18 and silicone from age 22 in the US.
Smooth implants tend to feel softer and move naturally but may ripple; textured implants are less likely to move but are where implant-associated ALCL occurs most often.
Round gives a fuller look with less concern about rotation; shaped implants give more controlled projection but can look unusual if they rotate and need a longer incision.
Profile determines how far the implant projects from the chest wall; it must match the width of your chest to look proportionate.

blocks.html:
Placement and incisions

The implant can sit under the pectoral muscle (submuscular) or behind the breast tissue over the muscle (subglandular). Access is usually through the inframammary fold (under the breast), around the areola, or in the armpit (transaxillary). The route affects scarring and, to some extent, how the implant behaves.

There is no single best combination. Nava and colleagues reviewed the evidence and found no high-level evidence identifying one ideal technique or implant; complication reduction follows established surgical principles rather than device fashion.

Longevity, monitoring and revision

Breast implants are not lifetime devices. There is no fixed lifespan: some remain stable for many years, but additional operations are common over a lifetime of implant use. For silicone implants, the US FDA recommends MRI or ultrasound screening five to six years after placement and then every two to three years, because a rupture can be silent.

Revision rates after primary augmentation have been reported as high as 36%, most commonly for capsular contracture, implant malposition and ptosis of the ageing breast. None of this means implants are unsafe — most people are satisfied — but it should shape expectations.

pages.h1: Breast Implant Safety: Rupture, ALCL, Contracture & Monitoring
pages.seoTitle: Breast Implant Safety: Rupture, ALCL, Contracture & Monitoring | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: What is actually known about breast implant safety — rupture and silent rupture, capsular contracture, BIA-ALCL, systemic symptoms, screening and the regulator guidance behind monitoring.
pages.bannerLead: Most people who have implants are satisfied, but implants have documented risks that do not disappear with time. This page sets out what the evidence and regulators actually say.

breadcrumb.label: Breast Implant Safety: Rupture, ALCL, Contracture & Monitoring

schema.name: Breast Implant Safety: Rupture, ALCL, Contracture & Monitoring

blocks.html: Implant safety is not a single yes-or-no. It is a set of known, quantified risks — some common and manageable, some rare and serious — against benefits that many patients find worthwhile. Reading them honestly is the basis of informed consent.

blocks.heading: What can happen, and how common it is
head: Risk
What it is
What to understand
rows: Tightening of the scar capsule around the implant
The most common reason for revision; can cause firmness, distortion and discomfort. Textured surfaces were introduced partly to reduce it.
Silicone rupture may cause no symptoms, which is why screening is recommended; saline rupture is usually obvious as the breast deflates.
Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma
A rare lymphoma of the fluid or capsule, linked mainly to textured implants. It is treatable, particularly when caught early.
A very rare cancer in the capsule; regulators list it alongside ALCL as a device-associated risk.
May require antibiotics and, in some cases, implant removal.
Self-reported fatigue, “brain fog”, joint pain and rash
Widely reported but not an established diagnosis; reviews find the correlation with implants is not established and evidence is limited.
Altered nipple or skin sensation; effects on feeding
Varies with technique and individual anatomy; discussed before consent.
Reported revision rates after primary augmentation are as high as 36%.

blocks.title: Monitoring, not reassurance
blocks.text: For silicone implants the FDA recommends MRI or ultrasound at five to six years after placement and then every two to three years, because a ruptured implant can produce no symptoms. Ongoing monitoring is part of living with implants — not a sign that something has gone wrong.

blocks.html:
What the systematic reviews show

The Cochrane Library holds independent systematic reviews and registered protocols on breast implants, wound drains, implant types and reconstruction. Systematic reviews pool many studies and sit at the top of the evidence ladder, which makes them the most reliable single guide to what is known and, equally importantly, to where the evidence is still missing.

The literature also documents past device failures and withdrawals — from PIP implants, with their increased rupture and leakage risk, to the soybean-oil-filled Trilucent implants that were withdrawn because of lipid-oxidation metabolites. These episodes are why modern regulators require long-term data and registries.

Injectable silicone and fillers

Importantly, most of the serious “breast filler” harms in the literature are not about implants at all. They concern injectable fillers and liquid silicone used to enlarge the breast off-label — products that can migrate, cause infection, granulomas and disfigurement, and interfere with mammography. The safest position on injectable fillers and silicone in the breast is the regulator position: do not use them for this purpose.

pages.h1: Breast Lift Surgery (Mastopexy): Shape, Scars & Longevity
pages.seoTitle: Breast Lift Surgery (Mastopexy): Shape, Scars & Longevity | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Breast lift (mastopexy): what it changes — sagging skin, nipple position and breast shape — how it differs from augmentation, scarring, longevity and combination options.
pages.bannerLead: A breast lift raises and reshapes sagging breasts by removing excess skin and repositioning the breast tissue and nipple. It changes shape, not volume.

breadcrumb.label: Breast Lift Surgery (Mastopexy): Shape, Scars & Longevity

schema.name: Breast Lift Surgery (Mastopexy): Shape, Scars & Longevity

blocks.html:
Sagging (ptosis) develops with ageing, pregnancy, breastfeeding, weight change and gravity. A breast lift addresses it by removing loose skin, reshaping the remaining breast tissue and repositioning the nipple–areola complex higher on the chest. Unlike augmentation, a lift on its own does not add volume — the breast is reshaped using the tissue already present.

The degree of lift required determines the pattern of scars: around the areola alone for mild sagging, plus a vertical line for moderate sagging, or an additional line within the inframammary fold for more significant sagging. Where more fullness is also desired, a lift can be combined with an implant or fat transfer, with the trade-offs of each discussed at consultation.

blocks.heading: What a lift changes — and what it cannot promise
blocks.body:
A mastopexy repositions the nipple–areola complex and reshapes the breast using the tissue already present. It can improve droop and projection, but it does not reliably add volume; where both shape and fullness need to change, a lift may be combined with an implant or fat transfer.

The scar pattern follows the amount of lift and skin tightening required: around the areola for a smaller lift, with a vertical line for a moderate lift, and sometimes an additional line within the inframammary fold. Scars soften and fade over months but remain permanent.

The reshaping can last many years, but it is not permanent. Pregnancy, weight change and ageing continue to affect the breast, and some people eventually choose further surgery.

items.title: Scars are permanent
items.text: Scars fade with time but do not disappear; their pattern depends on the lift required.

items.title: Results are long-lasting, not permanent
items.text: Pregnancy, weight change and ageing continue to affect the breast over time.

items.title: Combination is common
items.text: Lift with implant or fat transfer when both shape and volume need change.

items.title: Sensation and feeding
items.text: Nipple sensation and future breastfeeding may be affected; this is discussed in advance.

items.q: What is the difference between a breast lift and augmentation?
items.a: Augmentation adds volume with an implant or fat; a lift reshapes and raises existing tissue without adding volume. Some people need one, some need both, and the right combination depends on your anatomy and goals.

items.q: How long does a breast lift last?
items.a: The reshaping is durable, but the breast continues to age. Pregnancy, weight change and gravity gradually affect the result, and some people eventually choose further surgery.

items.q: Can a lift be done without visible scars?
items.a: No. Every lift technique involves incisions and therefore permanent scars, although they are planned to sit within the areola border or bra line. No procedure can promise scarless results.

pages.h1: Breast Revision Surgery: Implant Exchange, Removal & Repair
pages.seoTitle: Breast Revision Surgery: Implant Exchange, Removal & Repair | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Breast revision surgery: why implants may need revision — capsular contracture, rupture, displacement, asymmetry or a change in preferences — and what revision planning involves.
pages.bannerLead: Breast revision surgery is performed when a previous breast operation needs correction, adjustment or reversal — for example implant exchange, removal, or repair of capsule-related changes.

breadcrumb.label: Breast Revision Surgery: Implant Exchange, Removal & Repair

schema.name: Breast Revision Surgery: Implant Exchange, Removal & Repair

blocks.html:
Breast implants are not lifetime devices. Over time, the capsule of scar tissue that naturally forms around an implant can tighten (capsular contracture), an implant can rupture or change position, or the breasts can change with pregnancy, weight change and ageing. Some people also simply wish to change size. Revision surgery addresses any of these situations.

Revision is often more complex than a first operation: scar tissue, stretched skin, thinned breast tissue and previous implant position all shape what can safely be achieved. Planning should therefore be led by a suitably qualified surgeon who will examine you, review any previous operative records and imaging, and discuss realistic options — which may include implant exchange, removal with or without replacement, capsulectomy, or combining revision with a breast lift.

items.title: Capsular contracture
items.text: Scar tissue tightening around an implant, causing firmness, distortion or discomfort.

items.title: Implant rupture or deflation
items.text: Loss of implant integrity, confirmed by examination and imaging where indicated.

items.title: Position or shape changes
items.text: Displacement, rotation, bottoming out or an unnatural appearance over time.

items.title: Asymmetry
items.text: Differences between sides that developed after the original surgery.

items.title: Change of preference
items.text: A wish to change size, or to remove implants entirely (explantation).

items.title: Tissue changes
items.text: Sagging or skin laxity after pregnancy, weight change or ageing.

blocks.title: Revision is individualised
blocks.text: What is possible depends on the remaining breast tissue, skin quality, implant position and your goals. In some cases a good result requires combining implant revision with a breast lift, or accepting that implant removal alone will leave a less full shape.

items.q: How long do breast implants last?
items.a: There is no fixed lifespan. Implants may remain stable for many years, but additional operations are common over a lifetime of implant use. Regular review and prompt assessment of any new change are recommended.

items.q: Can implants be removed without replacement?
items.a: Yes — explantation without replacement is possible. The resulting shape depends on how much natural breast tissue remains and the degree of skin laxity; some people choose to combine removal with a lift.

items.q: Is revision surgery more complex than first-time surgery?
items.a: Often, yes. Existing scar tissue, altered anatomy and thinner breast tissue can make revision longer and less predictable. A thorough consultation, including imaging where indicated, is essential before planning.

pages.h1: Breast Filler Removal: Clearing Injected Fillers & Silicone
pages.seoTitle: Breast Filler Removal: Clearing Injected Fillers & Silicone | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Breast filler removal: why injected fillers and liquid silicone cause complications, how removal is approached, and what to expect regarding imaging, scars and staged treatment.
pages.bannerLead: Injectable fillers and liquid silicone are not approved for breast enlargement. When they cause pain, migration, lumps or infection, removal surgery may be required.

breadcrumb.label: Breast Filler Removal: Clearing Injected Fillers & Silicone

schema.name: Breast Filler Removal: Clearing Injected Fillers & Silicone

blocks.title: Fillers are not implants
blocks.text: Dermal fillers approved for facial use must never be assumed suitable for the breasts. Injected silicone and fillers can migrate, form granulomas, cause chronic inflammation and infection, and complicate breast imaging. They are not an equivalent or safer substitute for a breast implant.

blocks.html:
People who have had fillers or liquid silicone injected into the breasts may present with pain, hardness, migrating lumps, asymmetry, skin changes or recurrent infection. Removal is corrective surgery: the injected material is not neatly contained like an implant, and it interleaves with breast tissue, so complete removal is not always possible in one operation.

Surgical approaches may include removal of the injected material together with the surrounding affected tissue, staged procedures, and in some cases combining removal with implant placement or a lift once healthy tissue has healed. Imaging (such as ultrasound or mammography) is usually assessed before planning, because injected material can distort images and mask or mimic lesions.

items.title: Removal may be incomplete
items.text: Injected material spreads through tissue; complete clearance in one operation cannot be promised.

items.title: Imaging first
items.text: Breast imaging is typically reviewed before surgery to map the material and assess the tissue.

items.title: Staged treatment
items.text: More than one operation may be needed, with healing periods in between.

items.title: Scarring & shape
items.text: Removal can leave contour changes; reconstruction options are discussed case by case.

items.title: Pathology
items.text: Removed tissue may be sent for histological examination, as routine.

items.title: Delayed presentation
items.text: Complications can appear years after injection, so history matters at consultation.

items.q: Can all injected material be removed?
items.a: Not always. Injected silicone and fillers intermingle with breast tissue rather than sitting in a pocket, so complete removal in a single operation is not always achievable. The surgical aim is to remove as much affected material and tissue as safely possible.

items.q: Can implants be placed at the same time as removal?
items.a: Sometimes, but staged surgery is often safer when there is chronic inflammation or infection. Your surgeon will advise based on the condition of the tissue.

items.q: Do injected fillers affect breast screening?
items.a: Injected material can distort imaging and make interpretation harder. It is important to tell radiologists and surgeons about any prior injections, and to keep up with recommended screening.

pages.h1: Breast Reduction Surgery: Benefits, Techniques & Recovery
pages.seoTitle: Breast Reduction Surgery: Benefits, Techniques & Recovery | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Breast reduction surgery: how reducing breast volume and weight can relieve physical symptoms, what the procedure involves, scarring, recovery and factors that shape the outcome.
pages.bannerLead: Breast reduction removes skin, fat and glandular tissue to reduce breast size and weight, and repositions the breast into a more proportionate shape.

breadcrumb.label: Breast Reduction Surgery: Benefits, Techniques & Recovery

schema.name: Breast Reduction Surgery: Benefits, Techniques & Recovery

blocks.html:
Very large or heavy breasts can cause persistent neck, shoulder and back pain, shoulder-groove marks from bra straps, skin irritation beneath the breasts, and difficulty with physical activity. Breast reduction addresses both the symptoms and the proportions, by removing excess tissue and reshaping the remaining breast.

The operation is planned around your anatomy, the degree of reduction desired, blood supply to the nipple–areola complex and your overall health. Scarring is an unavoidable part of the procedure; incisions are placed so that scars fall within the bra line or along the areola border where possible. Because breast reduction is performed to relieve documented physical symptoms, it may in some cases be approached through medical insurance — criteria vary and require documentation.

items.title: Symptom relief
items.text: Reduction commonly relieves back, neck and shoulder strain caused by breast weight.

items.title: Scars are permanent
items.text: Incision lines around the areola, vertically, or along the inframammary fold.

items.title: Symmetry is approximate
items.text: Perfectly equal breasts cannot be promised; some asymmetry is normal.

items.title: Recovery period
items.text: Several weeks away from heavy lifting and exercise, with gradual return to activity.

items.title: Sensation changes
items.text: Nipple and breast skin sensation may temporarily or permanently change.

items.title: Breastfeeding
items.text: Future breastfeeding ability can be affected; this is discussed in advance.

blocks.heading: Incisions, tissue removal and reshaping
blocks.lead: Reduction removes glandular tissue, fat and skin, then reshapes the remaining breast and repositions the nipple–areola complex. The incision pattern depends on how much tissue is removed and how much lift is needed.
blocks.caption: Schematic areolar, vertical and inframammary incision patterns. Scars are permanent, although they usually fade and flatten over time.
blocks.note: Conceptual educational illustration; not a patient, treatment result or clinical recommendation.

blocks.heading: A gradual return to activity
blocks.lead: The first weeks focus on wound care, support and avoiding heavy lifting. Light daily activity usually resumes before strenuous exercise, and your surgeon’s aftercare instructions take priority over any general timeline.
blocks.caption: Conceptual recovery stages: early support and rest, a gradual return to light activity, then a phased return to exercise.
blocks.note: Individual healing, follow-up and activity restrictions vary; discuss them with your surgeon.

items.q: Can breast reduction be combined with a lift?
items.a: Breast reduction inherently includes lifting and reshaping the breast. A separate lift is generally not needed, although the specific technique is tailored to each case.

items.q: Will the breasts grow back after reduction?
items.a: Reduced tissue does not regrow, but substantial weight gain, pregnancy and hormonal changes can alter breast size again. Long-term results depend on stable weight and individual anatomy.

items.q: How much tissue is removed?
items.a: The amount depends on your anatomy, symptoms and goals, and is planned with your surgeon. The aim is a proportionate, symptom-relieving result rather than a specific cup size, which cannot be guaranteed.

pages.h1: Mastectomy & Chest Contouring Surgery: Patient Information
pages.seoTitle: Mastectomy & Chest Contouring Surgery: Patient Information | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Mastectomy and chest contouring: why surgery is performed, common approaches, recovery and questions for people considering mastectomy, gender-affirming chest surgery or gynaecomastia surgery.
pages.bannerLead: Mastectomy removes breast tissue. Chest contouring may follow mastectomy or be used for gender affirmation or gynaecomastia, with distinct techniques and goals.

breadcrumb.label: Mastectomy & Chest Contouring Surgery: Patient Information

schema.name: Mastectomy & Chest Contouring Surgery: Patient Information

blocks.html:
Mastectomy is the surgical removal of breast tissue. It is performed for several reasons, including gender-affirming chest masculinisation, reduction of elevated cancer risk in selected patients, and treatment of disease. Chest contouring is a broader term that can also include surgery for gynaecomastia. These are distinct operations with different medical purposes, even where some techniques overlap. This page provides general educational information; the appropriate procedure, eligibility and timing are determined through individual medical assessment.

When the goal is chest contouring rather than treatment of disease, the technique is tailored to the amount of breast tissue, skin laxity and the desired chest shape. Approaches may include a double-incision technique with nipple grafting, a periareolar (keyhole) approach in suitable anatomy, or gland excision and liposuction for gynaecomastia. The surgeon also considers scar placement, chest-wall contour and future revision options.

items.title: Which technique suits you
items.text: The approach depends on tissue volume, skin elasticity and the contour you want.

items.title: Scars and nipple position
items.text: Where incisions fall and how nipple–areola position and sensation are planned.

items.title: Risks
items.text: Bleeding, infection, contour irregularity, sensation changes and the possibility of revision.

items.title: Recovery
items.text: Drain use, compression garments, activity restrictions and follow-up schedule.

items.title: Eligibility assessment
items.text: Medical and psychological assessment where required, and any eligibility criteria that apply.

items.title: Future procedures
items.text: Whether staged or additional surgery may be needed to refine the result.

blocks.title: Assessment comes first
blocks.text: Chest surgery is elective and requires assessment by an appropriately qualified surgeon, including a discussion of risks, alternatives, realistic outcomes and — where required — eligibility criteria. No outcome can be guaranteed.

items.q: What is the difference between mastectomy and breast reduction?
items.a: Breast reduction removes a portion of tissue to make the breasts smaller while preserving a feminine breast shape. Mastectomy for chest contouring removes breast tissue to create a flatter, more masculine chest wall, with a different approach to nipple position and scars.

items.q: Will I need follow-up surgery?
items.a: Most people are satisfied with a single procedure, but refinement or revision surgery is sometimes desired for contour or scar reasons. This is discussed in advance.

items.q: How long is recovery?
items.a: Recovery varies with the technique and individual healing. Compression garments, limited arm activity and drain care are commonly required for a period after surgery, with a gradual return to full activity as advised by your surgeon.

pages.h1: Silicone vs Saline Breast Implants: What Is the Difference?
pages.seoTitle: Silicone vs Saline Breast Implants: Differences and Monitoring | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Compare silicone gel and saline breast implants, including feel, appearance, rupture detection, monitoring and questions to ask your surgeon.
pages.bannerLead: Both implant types use a silicone shell. The filling, how a leak shows up and the monitoring each needs are where they differ.
related: The wider guide to implant choices, surfaces and incisions.

blocks.html:
Breast implants have a silicone elastomer shell. The difference lies in what is inside. Neither type is automatically better, and the right choice depends on your tissue, preferences and willingness to follow long-term monitoring.

Saline implants

Saline implants are filled with sterile salt water. They can sometimes be filled during surgery, which may allow a smaller incision. If the shell leaks, the implant usually deflates visibly over a short time and the body absorbs the saline. Some people find saline implants feel firmer or show more rippling, especially with thin tissue coverage.

Silicone gel implants

Silicone gel implants are filled with cohesive silicone gel. Many people find the feel closer to natural breast tissue. If the shell is damaged, the gel often stays in place, so a rupture can go unnoticed. This is why regulators such as the US FDA recommend periodic imaging for silicone gel implants. FDA guidance suggests a first MRI scan around five to six years after surgery and then every two to three years. Ask your surgeon what is recommended where you live.

blocks.heading: How the two fillings compare
head: Consideration
Saline
Silicone gel
blocks.note: Individual anatomy, implant surface and placement also affect feel and appearance.

blocks.html:
Age and labelling

Implant labelling can set minimum ages. In the United States, saline implants are labelled for adults aged 18 and over and silicone gel implants for those aged 22 and over for cosmetic augmentation. Rules vary by country, so check the labelling and regulatory status where you are treated.

Questions to ask

  • Which implant type do you recommend for my tissue, and why?
  • What monitoring will I need, and who arranges it?
  • What is the manufacturer, model and warranty?
  • Will I receive an implant card with the batch details?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Neither type is better for everyone. The right choice depends on your anatomy, preferences and willingness to follow long-term monitoring. See the breast implants guide and breast implant safety.

pages.h1: Round vs Anatomical (Teardrop) Breast Implants
pages.seoTitle: Round vs Anatomical (Teardrop) Breast Implants | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Learn how round and teardrop-shaped breast implants differ in shape, rotation risk and appearance, and which questions help you choose.
pages.bannerLead: Implant shape affects how the upper and lower breast look. It also affects rotation risk and, in some cases, the implant surface used.
related: Why implant surface texture matters for safety.
How the filling changes feel and monitoring.

blocks.html:
Implant shape is a design choice, not a quality ranking. The right shape depends on your chest wall, the amount of soft tissue covering the implant and the look you want.

Round implants

Round implants are uniformly rounded, with fullness at the top and bottom. If they rotate slightly, the shape usually looks the same. They are available in smooth surfaces and some textured options.

Anatomical (teardrop) implants

Anatomical implants are shaped with a gentle slope at the top and more volume at the bottom, resembling a natural breast. Because they have a defined shape, rotation can change the look of the breast. They have historically been textured to reduce rotation.

Texture matters for safety

Some textured implants have been linked to a rare lymphoma called BIA-ALCL. Regulators in several countries have restricted certain textured implants. Ask your surgeon specifically about the surface texture of any implant proposed, and read our page on BIA-ALCL and breast implant illness.

Which looks more natural?

This depends on your chest shape and tissue. Many people with enough soft-tissue coverage get a natural result with round implants, because the breast tissue itself shapes the upper slope. Very thin tissue may show the implant outline more, whichever shape is used.

Questions to ask

  • Why do you recommend this shape for me?
  • What is the surface texture and its safety record?
  • What is the chance of rotation or displacement?
  • Which manufacturer and model, and how long has it been on the market?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Shape is a design choice, not a guarantee of a natural result. Prioritise safety information and your own anatomy over trends.

pages.h1: How to Choose Breast Implant Size Realistically
pages.seoTitle: How to Choose Breast Implant Size Realistically | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Why cup size is unreliable, how surgeons assess implant volume, and what to consider so your expectations match your anatomy.
pages.bannerLead: Cup sizes vary between brands and countries. Implants are measured in volume, and the same volume looks different on different bodies.
related: How size, profile and base width interact.
What revision can and cannot change.

blocks.html:
Many people start with a cup size in mind, but cup sizes vary between brands and countries. Implants are measured in cubic centimetres (cc), and the same volume looks different on different bodies.

What influences the right size

  • Chest width and breast base width
  • Existing breast volume and shape
  • Skin elasticity and the soft tissue available to cover the implant
  • Body proportions and height
  • Your goals and lifestyle, including exercise

Why bigger is not always better

Larger implants place more stretch and weight on tissues. They can increase the chance of visible rippling, thinning of tissue, sagging over time and further surgery. A size that looks good in a photograph may not suit your tissue.

Tools that help

Surgeons may use sizers placed inside a bra, measurements of the breast base and 3D simulations. Treat simulations as a rough guide only, because they cannot predict how your tissues will heal and settle.

How to communicate your goals

  • Use photos to show the look you want, not just a size
  • Bring pictures of results you do not want
  • Ask the surgeon to explain which of your wishes your anatomy supports

Settling

Swelling means that the size you see in the first weeks is not the final result. Implants also settle over time. Ask when your surgeon expects the result to stabilise and what changes are normal.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: The best size is the one your tissues can support with the lowest long-term risk. A qualified surgeon can help you estimate that, but no simulation can guarantee a result. See breast augmentation.

pages.bannerLead: An implant can sit in different layers of the chest. The choice affects how natural the result looks, how it feels, recovery and some long-term risks.
related: The wider guide to implant planning.

Position
Trade-offs

What influences the choice

  • Implant size and type
  • Your activity level, for example regular weight training

Questions to ask

  • Which placement do you recommend for my body, and why?
  • What are the drawbacks of that option for me?
  • How often do you perform it?

blocks.text: Placement is a surgical decision with trade-offs, not a loyalty test for one technique. Ask for the reasoning specific to your anatomy. See breast implants.

pages.h1: How Long Do Breast Implants Last?
pages.seoTitle: How Long Do Breast Implants Last? | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Breast implants are not lifetime devices. Learn what affects their lifespan, why monitoring matters and when replacement or removal may be needed.
pages.bannerLead: Implants are long-term medical devices, not a one-time purchase. Many people need further surgery at some point, although timing varies widely.
related: The wider guide to implant choice and follow-up.
A common reason for revision surgery.

blocks.html:
A common question is whether implants last forever. The accurate answer is no. Breast implants are medical devices, and regulators such as the US FDA state that they are not lifetime devices. Many people will need further surgery at some point, although timing varies widely.

Why implants may need replacing or removing

  • Rupture or leakage of the shell
  • Capsular contracture, where scar tissue tightens around the implant
  • Changes in breast shape from ageing, weight change, pregnancy or breastfeeding
  • Implant displacement or rotation
  • Visible rippling or edge visibility
  • Personal preference for a different size
  • Rarely, a serious complication that needs removal

The longer you have them, the more likely a problem

The chance of complications generally rises with time. Studies by manufacturers and independent researchers report a meaningful proportion of people having further surgery within ten years, though figures differ by implant type and study.

Monitoring

For silicone gel implants, a rupture may produce few symptoms. The US FDA recommends MRI screening about five to six years after surgery and then every two to three years; ultrasound may be used where MRI is unsuitable or unavailable. Ask your surgeon what monitoring applies in your country. For all implants, report new pain, swelling, a change in shape or firmness, or lumps.

Keep your records

Keep your implant card with the manufacturer, model, size and batch number. This helps if recalls, safety notices or future surgery arise.

Planning for the long term

Before surgery, ask about the likelihood of revision, the costs of monitoring and replacement, and the clinic’s policy if you need another operation.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Think of implants as long-term devices that need ongoing attention, not a one-time procedure. See breast revision surgery and breast implant safety.

pages.h1: Capsular Contracture Explained
pages.seoTitle: Capsular Contracture After Breast Implants | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: What capsular contracture is, how it is graded, possible causes, symptoms and treatment options after breast implant surgery.
pages.bannerLead: A capsule of scar tissue forms around every implant. Contracture happens when that capsule tightens and squeezes the implant.
related: Why revision may be needed over time.

blocks.html:
Whenever the body has a foreign object, it forms a thin layer of scar tissue around it, called a capsule. This is normal. Capsular contracture happens when that capsule tightens and thickens, squeezing the implant.

What it can feel like

  • A firmer breast
  • A change in shape, with the implant looking rounder, higher or distorted
  • Discomfort or pain
  • In advanced cases, a hard, painful breast

The Baker grading

Surgeons often describe severity using four grades. The grade is a clinical description, not a prediction of what will happen next.

blocks.heading: The Baker scale
head: Grade
What it describes
rows: Breast is soft and looks natural

blocks.html:
What causes it?

The exact cause is not fully understood. Factors that have been studied include bacterial contamination around the implant (biofilm), bleeding or fluid collection after surgery, infection, radiation therapy and implant characteristics. It can develop soon after surgery or years later.

How it is managed

Options depend on severity and your preferences. They can include observation for mild cases and surgery for more severe ones, such as removing the capsule (capsulectomy), replacing the implant or removing it altogether. Contracture can return after treatment.

Reducing risk

Surgeons use techniques intended to lower the chance, such as careful control of bleeding, minimising contamination and appropriate pocket choice. No technique guarantees prevention.

When to seek review

Tell your surgeon if one breast becomes firmer, changes shape or becomes painful. Early review gives more options.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Capsular contracture is a known and relatively common reason for revision surgery. Ask any surgeon you consult how often they see it and how they manage it. See breast implant safety.

pages.h1: BIA-ALCL and Breast Implant Illness: What the Evidence Says
pages.seoTitle: BIA-ALCL and Breast Implant Illness: What the Evidence Says | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: A calm, factual explanation of BIA-ALCL and breast implant illness, what is known, what is uncertain and when to talk to a doctor.
pages.bannerLead: Two topics often cause worry: BIA-ALCL and what people call breast implant illness. They are different, and the evidence differs too.

blocks.html:
BIA-ALCL is a rare cancer of immune system cells linked to breast implants. “Breast implant illness” is a term used for a group of symptoms some people attribute to their implants. They should not be confused with each other.

BIA-ALCL

Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma is a rare cancer of immune system cells, not of breast tissue. It has been linked mostly to textured implants. It most often appears years after surgery, commonly as sudden swelling from fluid around the implant, or sometimes as a lump or capsule thickening. When found early and confined to the capsule, it is usually treated by surgery to remove the implant and the surrounding capsule, with other treatment in more advanced cases.

Several regulators have restricted or withdrawn certain textured implants after reviewing the association. Ask your surgeon what the surface of any implant is, and which regulatory approvals it holds.

What to watch for

  • Swelling of one breast that appears long after surgery
  • A new lump in the breast or armpit
  • Pain, redness or changes in the breast

If you notice these, see a doctor and mention your implants.

Breast implant illness

Some people with implants report symptoms such as fatigue, joint pain, brain fog, rashes and anxiety and attribute them to their implants. It is not currently an established medical diagnosis, and research has not found a single clear mechanism. Many people report improvement after implant removal, though studies cannot yet say how much of this is due to the implants themselves. Symptoms are real and deserve a proper medical assessment to look for other causes.

How to approach this as a patient

  • Ask about the implant surface and the manufacturer’s safety record
  • Ask how the clinic follows up long term
  • Keep your implant documentation
  • Do not ignore symptoms, and do not assume they are unrelated

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Serious implant-associated lymphoma is rare but real, and honest counselling should mention it. See breast implant safety and our research library.

pages.h1: Breast Implants and Mammograms: What You Should Know
pages.seoTitle: Breast Implants and Mammograms: What You Should Know | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: How breast implants affect mammograms and breast screening, what to tell the imaging team and why screening still matters.
pages.bannerLead: Having implants does not mean you should skip breast screening. It does mean that imaging may need to be adapted.

blocks.html:
Implants can make mammograms more complex, but they do not make screening unimportant. Tell the imaging team about your implants when you book and when you attend.

Do implants cause breast cancer?

Major reviews have not found that implants cause breast cancer in breast tissue. Separately, rare implant-associated lymphoma is discussed on our BIA-ALCL page.

How implants affect mammograms

Implants can block part of the breast from view on a standard mammogram, because X-rays do not pass through them well. Imaging teams therefore often take additional views that gently push the implant back and pull breast tissue forward, called implant displacement views. Compression can feel uncomfortable, and in rare cases may risk implant damage.

What to do

  • Tell the clinic you have implants when booking
  • Ask whether the facility has experience with implant imaging
  • Bring your implant card
  • Mention where the implant is placed and any history of capsular contracture or rupture

Other imaging

Ultrasound and MRI may be used in addition to mammograms. MRI is also used to check silicone implants for rupture in some patients.

Surgery planning and screening

Before augmentation, a baseline mammogram or other screening may be recommended depending on your age and risk. Follow your doctor’s advice and national guidelines.

Symptoms

Self-examination matters. Know what your breasts normally look and feel like, and report new lumps, skin changes, nipple discharge or persistent pain.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Implants make screening a little more complex, not less important. See breast enlargement safety.

pages.h1: Breast Augmentation, Pregnancy and Breastfeeding
pages.seoTitle: Breast Augmentation, Pregnancy and Breastfeeding | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: How breast augmentation may affect pregnancy, breastfeeding and breast shape, and what to consider if you plan to have children.
pages.bannerLead: Many people considering augmentation also plan to have children. The two interact in a few ways, and timing is worth discussing openly.
related: A different set of pregnancy considerations.
How a lift addresses shape after pregnancy.

blocks.html:
Many people considering augmentation also plan to have children. The two interact in a few ways, and there is no single timeline that suits everyone.

Can I breastfeed with implants?

Many people with implants breastfeed successfully, but it is not guaranteed. Factors include the incision, the implant position, whether nerves or ducts were affected, and your breast tissue before surgery. Incisions around the nipple may carry a higher chance of affecting milk supply. A person who has had implants may also have had limited glandular tissue to begin with.

Is breastfeeding safe for the baby?

Current evidence has not shown that silicone from intact implants passes into milk at harmful levels. If you have concerns, discuss them with your doctor.

How pregnancy changes breasts

Breast size and shape change during pregnancy and breastfeeding, with or without implants. Skin stretches, and breasts may look different afterwards. Implants do not prevent these changes, and surgery before pregnancy may mean a lift, revision or other procedure later.

Timing

Some surgeons recommend waiting until you have finished having children. Others operate earlier if the person understands that further surgery may be needed. Fat transfer and implants have different considerations, which you can read about on our fat transfer page.

Surgery during pregnancy or breastfeeding

Elective breast surgery is generally not done during pregnancy or while breastfeeding. Surgeons usually advise waiting some months after you stop breastfeeding.

Questions to ask

  • Which incision best protects breastfeeding for me?
  • How will pregnancy affect my result?
  • What is the likelihood of needing a lift or revision afterwards?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: If pregnancy is likely in the near future, discuss timing openly with your surgeon before deciding. See breast augmentation.

pages.h1: Fat Transfer: How Much Fat Actually Survives?
pages.seoTitle: Fat Transfer: How Much Fat Actually Survives? | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Why fat survival after breast fat transfer varies, what affects it, how many sessions may be needed and how to set realistic expectations.
pages.bannerLead: Fat transfer uses your own fat, but not all of the transferred fat survives. Published retention rates vary widely, and individual results are unpredictable.
related: Fat transfer against implants and other approaches.

blocks.html:
Fat transfer uses your own fat, collected by liposuction, processed and injected into the breasts. A common question is how much of that fat remains.

Not all of it survives

Transferred fat needs a blood supply to survive. Some fat cells establish one; others do not and are absorbed by the body. Published studies report a wide range of retention, and individual results are unpredictable. Be wary of any provider promising a fixed percentage.

What may influence survival

  • The technique used to harvest, process and inject fat
  • The volume injected, since too much at once can reduce survival
  • Your tissue and skin elasticity
  • Smoking, which affects blood supply
  • Weight change after surgery
  • Whether a bra or external expansion device is used before surgery, which some surgeons use

Realistic volume

Fat transfer typically offers a modest, natural-feeling increase rather than a dramatic one. Some people need more than one session to reach their goal.

Possible complications

These include uneven results, fat necrosis (areas of hardened fat), oil cysts and calcifications that can show up on breast imaging, infection and the usual risks of liposuction. Tell any imaging team you have had fat transfer.

Who may not be suitable

People with little donor fat, or who want a large increase in size, may find it does not meet their goals. Your surgeon should explain this honestly.

Questions to ask

  • How much do you expect to survive in someone like me?
  • How many sessions might I need?
  • How do you handle lumps or calcifications?
  • Do you have results from patients with a similar body type?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Fat transfer can be a good option for modest change, but expectations should be set around variability. See fat transfer breast augmentation.

pages.h1: Breast Lift vs Breast Augmentation: Which Do You Need?
pages.seoTitle: Breast Lift vs Breast Augmentation: Which Do You Need? | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Understand the difference between a breast lift and augmentation, when each is used, and when they are combined.
pages.bannerLead: People often say they want “bigger” or “perkier” breasts without being sure which procedure achieves that. The two operations solve different problems.
related: What revision can change after either procedure.

blocks.html:
Augmentation adds volume. A lift changes position and shape. Some people need one, some need the other, and some need both.

What augmentation does

Breast augmentation adds volume, using implants or fat transfer. It can improve fullness and proportions but does not remove excess skin. If breasts already sag, adding volume can sometimes make the sagging more obvious.

What a breast lift does

A breast lift (mastopexy) raises the breast and reshapes it by removing excess skin and tightening the surrounding tissue. It repositions the nipple higher. It does not add significant volume. See breast lift surgery.

How sagging is assessed

Surgeons assess breast ptosis by looking at the position of the nipple relative to the fold beneath the breast. The more the breast and nipple sit below that fold, the more likely a lift is needed.

When a combination is considered

If you have both low volume and sagging, you may be offered a lift with augmentation. Some surgeons perform both in one operation, and others stage them in two steps because the combination carries higher risks, such as problems with healing or implant position.

Trade-offs

  • A lift leaves scars, usually around the nipple, and often down and along the fold, depending on the technique
  • Results are not permanent, because gravity and ageing continue
  • Combined surgery may mean a longer operation and recovery

Questions to ask

  • Do I need a lift, augmentation or both, and why?
  • What scars should I expect and where?
  • If you advise staging, what is the reason?
  • What is the chance I will need revision?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Volume and position are separate problems. A thorough assessment, not a guess from photos, decides which operation fits. See breast lift and breast augmentation.

pages.h1: Breast Asymmetry: What Is Normal and What Can Be Done
pages.seoTitle: Breast Asymmetry: What Is Normal and What Can Be Done | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Most people have some breast asymmetry. Learn what is normal, what causes larger differences and what options exist.
pages.bannerLead: Breasts are rarely perfect mirror images. Small differences in size, shape, nipple position and the breast fold are very common.
related: Reducing volume on one or both sides.
Using your own fat to build up the smaller breast.

blocks.html:
Small differences in size, shape, nipple position and the breast fold are very common, and many people never notice them. A new or rapidly changing difference needs medical assessment.

Why asymmetry happens

  • Natural variation in development during puberty
  • Differences in the chest wall or spine, including mild curvature
  • Hormonal changes, pregnancy and breastfeeding, which may affect each breast differently
  • Weight changes
  • Previous surgery, injury or radiotherapy
  • Congenital conditions, for example tuberous breast shape or chest wall differences

When to see a doctor

A new change in one breast, such as a lump, skin change, nipple discharge or sudden size difference, needs medical assessment. Asymmetry that has always been present is usually not a health concern, but a clinician can check for underlying causes if it is marked or you are worried.

Options when it bothers you

  • Implants of different sizes
  • Fat transfer to build up the smaller breast
  • A breast lift or reduction on one or both sides
  • A combination of procedures

Surgery can improve symmetry but cannot make breasts identical. Implants also settle differently, and breasts may change differently over time.

Non-surgical options

Padded or shaped bras and prostheses can balance appearance without surgery. Injectables are not a safe solution. See unsafe breast injections.

Questions to ask

  • Is my asymmetry normal or does it suggest an underlying condition?
  • Which options fit my anatomy?
  • How closely can the result match, realistically?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Some asymmetry is normal. If it affects your confidence, there are options, but realistic expectations matter. See breast enlargement safety for warning signs.

pages.h1: After Breast Surgery or Injection: Warning Signs That Need Urgent Attention
pages.seoTitle: Warning Signs After Breast Surgery or Injection | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Know the symptoms after breast surgery, fat transfer or injections that need urgent medical care, and what to do next.
pages.bannerLead: Most recoveries go as expected, but some symptoms need prompt assessment. This page is general information, not a substitute for your surgical team’s instructions.
related: A later cause of firmness or pain.

blocks.html:
If in doubt, call your surgical team or seek emergency care. A prompt call is better than waiting to see if a symptom passes.

Seek emergency care now if you have

  • Chest pain, difficulty breathing or coughing blood, which can signal a blood clot in the lungs
  • Fainting, extreme dizziness or confusion
  • Rapid, painful swelling of one breast, which may mean bleeding
  • Signs of severe allergic reaction, such as swelling of the face or throat

Contact your surgeon or a doctor urgently if you notice

  • Fever or chills
  • Spreading redness, warmth or pus from a wound
  • Increasing pain that is not controlled with prescribed medicine
  • A wound opening
  • Swelling, pain or redness in one calf, which can signal a clot
  • Skin turning dark, pale, blue or blistered
  • An implant that seems to have moved, or a sudden change in shape or size

After injections into the breast

  • Severe pain or skin colour change soon after the injection
  • Hard, tender or growing lumps
  • Redness, heat or discharge

Tell clinicians exactly what was injected, if you know.

Late problems

Symptoms can also appear months or years later, such as new swelling of one breast, a firm breast, a lump or pain. See our pages on capsular contracture and BIA-ALCL.

Be prepared

  • Save your surgeon’s and the facility’s emergency number
  • Know the nearest hospital with emergency services
  • Keep your implant card and a list of your medicines
  • Ask before surgery who you should contact after hours

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Act early. A prompt call is better than waiting to see if a symptom passes. See breast enlargement safety.

pages.h1: Who Is a Good Candidate for Breast Augmentation?
pages.seoTitle: Who Is a Good Candidate for Breast Augmentation? | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Understand who may be suitable for breast augmentation, who may need to wait, and the health and expectation factors a surgeon assesses.
pages.bannerLead: Suitability is about health, anatomy and motivation as much as size. A good consultation includes an honest discussion of when surgery is not the right step.
related: The parent guide to planning, surgery and recovery.
Questions and information to prepare before you decide.
When sagging, rather than volume, is the main concern.

blocks.html:
Breast augmentation is elective surgery, so suitability depends on your health, anatomy and reasons for wanting it. Only a qualified surgeon can assess this in person, but the points below explain what is usually considered.

Factors that often support candidacy

  • You are an adult in good general health.
  • Your breasts have finished developing, or you are unhappy with volume after pregnancy, weight loss or natural change.
  • You want the change for yourself, not mainly to please someone else.
  • Your expectations are realistic and you understand the risks.
  • You accept that further surgery may be needed at some point.

What the surgeon examines

  • Breast width, volume, shape and skin elasticity.
  • Nipple position and the level of the breast fold.
  • Chest-wall shape and any asymmetry.
  • The thickness of soft tissue available to cover an implant.
  • Whether sagging suggests a breast lift may be needed instead of, or as well as, augmentation.

When surgery may need to wait or may not suit

  • Pregnancy or breastfeeding.
  • An active infection, or an unexplained breast lump that has not been assessed.
  • Poorly controlled medical conditions, including bleeding disorders.
  • Smoking or nicotine use, which can slow healing.
  • Plans for pregnancy in the near future, which some surgeons advise waiting for.
  • Significant distress about appearance that seems out of proportion to what others see; a good surgeon may suggest speaking to a mental health professional first.
  • Expectations that surgery cannot meet.

Age, consent and expectations

Implant labelling includes minimum ages in some countries, and surgeons are generally cautious about operating before breast development is complete. There is no single upper age limit; general health and tissue quality matter more. A useful consultation should tell you not only whether you are suitable, but which approach is suitable and why.

What surgery can and cannot change

Augmentation can add volume and alter upper-breast fullness. It cannot change your height, waist, skin quality or the underlying shape of your chest wall, and it will not make your breasts symmetrical if the asymmetry comes from the ribcage or the position of the fold. A lift is better for sagging; reduction removes tissue. Understanding these limits before surgery is more useful than comparing cup sizes.

Questions to ask

  • Am I a suitable candidate, and for which approach?
  • What would make me unsuitable?
  • Would waiting, a lift or another option be better for me?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A good consultation includes being told when surgery is not the right step. That is part of careful assessment, not a reason to feel rejected. Read the breast augmentation guide for the wider picture.
