pages.h1: Breast Augmentation Step by Step: Before, During and After
pages.seoTitle: Breast Augmentation Step by Step: Before, During and After | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: A plain-language walkthrough of breast augmentation, from the consultation and anaesthesia to the operation, recovery and follow-up.
pages.bannerLead: Knowing the stages helps you ask better questions. Details vary by surgeon and facility, and your own team’s instructions come first.
related: The parent guide to benefits, risks and recovery.
Practical checks, medicines and home arrangements.
How swelling, settling and long-term change affect the look.

blocks.html:
Breast augmentation is a planned operation with several stages. Understanding them can reduce uncertainty and help you compare what different clinics offer.

1. Consultation and planning

You discuss your goals, health history and options, and the surgeon measures and examines you. You should receive written information and time to decide. A second consultation is reasonable if you are unsure.

2. Pre-operative assessment

This may include a medical review and blood tests, plus instructions about medicines and fasting. Any breast lump or abnormal screening result should be assessed before surgery. See preparing for breast augmentation.

3. Anaesthesia

Most augmentations are performed under general anaesthesia, given by a qualified anaesthetist. Ask who will monitor you throughout and what emergency equipment and arrangements are available.

4. The operation

The surgeon makes an incision, creates a pocket for the implant, places the implant and closes the wound. Operation time commonly ranges from about one to two hours, but varies with the plan and whether other procedures are combined. Drains are used in some cases.

5. Immediate recovery

You wake in a recovery area, usually with dressings and a supportive garment. Many people go home the same day or after one night, depending on the facility and how they recover.

6. First days and weeks

Expect soreness, swelling, bruising and tightness. Follow instructions on medicines, rest, wound care and lifting restrictions. Contact the team early if pain, swelling or redness worsens rather than waiting for a routine review.

What can vary between clinics

Not every augmentation follows the same pathway. The facility, anaesthetic team, implant choice, use of drains, garment, follow-up schedule and arrangements for complications can all differ. Ask who performs the operation, who provides anaesthesia, what is included in the quoted cost, and what happens if you need unplanned care. A lower price may exclude follow-up or revision. These details matter more than a hotel-style brochure.

7. Follow-up and long-term care

Check-ups monitor healing and implant position. Ask how many are included, how to reach the team out of hours, and what monitoring is advised for your implant type. Keep your implant card and report any new change in shape, size or comfort.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: The operation is only one part of the process. Planning, consent and aftercare matter as much, and a clear route for urgent questions is part of safe care.

blocks.html: The incision is a surgical access route, not a cosmetic add-on. The right choice depends on your anatomy, the implant, your surgeon’s experience and what matters most to you.

blocks.heading: Where the scar sits and what it means
head: Route
Position
Trade-offs
rows: In the fold beneath the breast
Direct access and widely used. The scar is usually hidden in the fold, though it can be visible when lying down or if the fold position changes.
Around the lower edge of the areola
Scars can blend well where skin colour changes. Some evidence links this route to more nipple-sensation changes, and larger implants can be harder to place through a small opening.
No scar on the breast, but access to the pocket is more limited and a camera may be used. Placement can be harder to control and revision through the same route can be difficult.
blocks.note: A cut through the navel (transumbilical) has been used with saline implants but is less common and offers less control. Ask about your surgeon’s experience with any technique.

blocks.html:
How to compare the options

Ask your surgeon to explain what each route would mean for your implant size, your tissue and any future revision. A scar in a less visible place is not automatically the safer choice if it limits access or makes the pocket harder to control. Write down the trade-offs in your own words, and take the plan home before deciding.

Other factors in choosing

  • Implant type, surface and size.
  • Your skin quality and how you tend to scar.
  • Whether you plan to breastfeed.
  • Your surgeon’s training and usual practice.
  • The possible need for future revision.

Scarring

Scars fade over many months but never disappear. People vary widely in how they scar. Follow aftercare advice, avoid sun exposure on healing scars, and report a scar that becomes raised, painful or keeps growing. Massage, silicone gel sheets and other scar treatments are sometimes advised, but evidence for them is limited. Ask before using anything on a healing wound.

Questions to ask

  • Which incision do you recommend for me, and why?
  • Where exactly will the scar be, and how long will it be?
  • How would this affect revision later?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Choose the incision on safety and suitability first, scar position second. See the breast augmentation guide.

pages.h1: Preparing for Breast Augmentation: A Practical Checklist
pages.seoTitle: Preparing for Breast Augmentation: A Practical Checklist | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: How to prepare for breast augmentation, covering medical checks, medicines, smoking, home preparation and what to arrange for recovery.
pages.bannerLead: Good preparation can reduce stress and may help recovery. Always follow your surgeon’s own instructions where they differ from this general guide.
related: What happens from anaesthesia to follow-up.
Questions to ask before committing to surgery.
Symptoms that need prompt medical assessment.

blocks.html:
Preparation is not only about the day of surgery. It covers your health, medicines, home setup and the support you will need while you recover.

Health checks

  • A full medical-history review and any tests your surgeon requests.
  • Breast screening or imaging if advised for your age and risk.
  • Management of conditions such as high blood pressure or diabetes.
  • Assessment of any breast lump or unusual change before surgery.

Medicines and supplements

Tell your team about everything you take, including over-the-counter products and herbal supplements. Some medicines, such as blood thinners and anti-inflammatories, and some supplements can increase bleeding risk, and you may be asked to stop them before surgery. Do not stop prescribed medicines without advice.

Smoking and nicotine

Smoking and nicotine products reduce blood flow and can slow healing and increase wound complications. Surgeons often ask you to stop for several weeks before and after surgery. Ask for support if you need it.

Fasting and the day before

You will be told when to stop eating and drinking before anaesthesia. Follow this exactly. If you become unwell, contact the facility before travelling.

Practical arrangements

  • A responsible adult to take you home and stay with you for the first day or two.
  • Time off work, based on your surgeon’s advice and the demands of your job.
  • Front-opening tops and loose clothing.
  • Prescribed medicines collected in advance.
  • Extra pillows so you can rest comfortably.
  • Help with childcare, lifting and housework.
  • Your surgeon’s emergency contact saved in your phone.

The week before surgery

Confirm your admission time, fasting instructions and transport. Check that your medicines and aftercare supplies are ready, and tell your employer what you have arranged. Avoid starting new supplements or treatments in the days before surgery, and do not shave or apply products to the chest unless your team advises it.

When to reschedule

Contact the facility if you develop a fever, a chest infection, a skin infection or any illness that could affect anaesthesia. It is safer to postpone than to proceed while unwell.

Mental preparation

It is normal to feel nervous. Swelling means your breasts will not look final in the first weeks, so plan for patience and avoid judging the result too early.

Questions to ask

  • Which medicines should I stop, and when?
  • What should I bring on the day?
  • Who do I call if I have a problem at night?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Follow instructions carefully and arrange support at home before you go in. See the consultation checklist for the questions to settle first.

pages.h1: Breast Augmentation Results Over Time: Year One and Beyond
pages.seoTitle: Breast Augmentation Results Over Time: Year One and Beyond | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: How breast augmentation results change from the first weeks to years later, including swelling, settling, ageing and weight change.
pages.bannerLead: Augmentation is not a one-off event with a fixed result. Swelling, healing, ageing and body change all affect how the breasts look.
related: The parent guide to planning and recovery.
Exchange, removal and repair when a result changes.

blocks.html:
The result you see in the first weeks is not the final result. Breasts and implants continue to change with healing, ageing and changes in body weight.

First weeks

Swelling and bruising are common. Implants may sit high and feel tight, and muscle tightness can limit movement at first. Early photographs are not a reliable guide to the final look.

Three to six months

Swelling reduces and implants usually drop and settle into position. Scars are still maturing and may look red or raised before fading. Many surgeons reassess around this time.

One year

Most people see the closest picture of their settled result around a year after surgery, although change continues. If you are unhappy, wait until the result has stabilised before discussing revision.

Judging the result

Compare like with like: use the same lighting, posture and camera angle, and avoid judging in the first three months. Ask your surgeon what changes are expected at each review. A result that looks slightly uneven while healing may settle, but a change that appears after months of stability deserves assessment. Photographs can show proportions but not how the breasts feel, move or age.

When to discuss revision

Revision is easier to plan once the tissues have settled. Bring specific concerns, such as width, upper fullness or nipple position, rather than a single photograph of someone else.

Long term

Breasts and implants continue to change with:

  • Ageing and gravity, which affect skin and tissue even with implants.
  • Weight gain or loss, which changes the soft tissue around the implant.
  • Pregnancy and breastfeeding.
  • Hormonal changes such as menopause.
  • Time, since implants may shift, wear or need replacement.

Possible later changes include visible rippling, altered firmness, displacement and a wish for a different size. Some people need further surgery, such as a lift or revision. See how long implants last.

Looking after the result

  • Attend follow-up visits and any recommended imaging.
  • Wear supportive bras as advised.
  • Maintain a stable weight where possible.
  • Protect scars from sun.
  • Report any new change promptly.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Think of augmentation as the beginning of a long-term relationship with your implants and your breast health, not a single finished result. See the breast augmentation guide.

pages.h1: How Breast Implants Are Made and Regulated
pages.seoTitle: How Breast Implants Are Made and Regulated | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: What breast implants are made of, how they are regulated as medical devices, and why knowing the manufacturer and model matters.
pages.bannerLead: Breast implants are medical devices, not cosmetic products. Understanding how they are made and overseen helps you ask the right questions.
related: Types, surfaces, placement and long-term reality.
Cards, registries, recalls and what cover usually means.

blocks.html:
A breast implant is a regulated medical device. Knowing what it is made of, who made it and where it is approved is part of informed consent.

Structure

An implant has an outer shell and a filling.

  • Shell: a layered silicone elastomer, which may have a smooth or textured surface.
  • Filling: sterile saline or cohesive silicone gel.
  • Features: some have a valve, a barrier layer intended to limit gel bleed, or a defined anatomical shape.

Manufacturing and quality

Reputable manufacturers produce implants under quality-management systems, test shell strength and gel properties, and track each implant by a batch or lot number. That traceability is what makes a recall or warranty claim possible.

What “cohesive” means

Cohesive gel is designed to hold together rather than flow like liquid. It can still leak if the shell fails, and it is not the same as injectable silicone. The term describes the filling’s behaviour, not a guarantee that rupture will always be obvious.

Regulation

Regulators decide whether a device may be sold and what evidence is required. In the United States, the FDA reviews breast implants through a premarket approval process. In Europe, devices carry a CE mark under medical-device regulations. In India, medical devices are governed by the Medical Devices Rules and overseen by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO); CDSCO classification material lists breast implants as Class C. Check the current classification and licensing status for the exact product with CDSCO before publication or surgery. Approval in one country does not guarantee the same status elsewhere.

Approval is a minimum standard, not a promise of perfect performance. It reflects the evidence available at the time and comes with conditions for monitoring and reporting.

Why the manufacturer matters

  • Track record and published long-term safety data.
  • Whether the model has been recalled or restricted.
  • Warranty and support terms.
  • Traceability if a problem occurs.

Warning signs

Be cautious if the clinic cannot name the manufacturer and model, cannot show approvals, offers unbranded or “imported” implants without documentation, or will not give you an implant card.

Questions to ask

  • Who manufactures the implant, and what is the exact model?
  • Where is it approved, and can I see the documentation?
  • What long-term data exist for this model?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: The implant is a regulated device. You are entitled to know exactly what is placed in your body, who made it and how it is traced. See breast implants.

pages.h1: Implant Profile, Width and Volume Explained
pages.seoTitle: Breast Implant Profile, Width and Volume Explained | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: How implant profile, base width and volume work together to determine how a breast implant looks, and why volume alone is a poor guide.
pages.bannerLead: Two implants with the same volume can look very different. Surgeons use several measurements to choose an implant that suits your body.
related: Why cup size is unreliable and how volume is assessed.
The wider guide to implant choices.
How the pocket and muscle affect the final look.

blocks.html:
Implant size is not just a number of cubic centimetres. Width, projection and volume interact, and the right balance depends on your chest and soft tissue.

Volume

Volume is measured in cubic centimetres (cc). It describes how much the implant holds, not how large it will look on you. The same volume can look modest on a wider chest and fuller on a narrower one.

Base width

Base width is the measurement across the bottom of the implant. It should fit the width of your breast so that the implant does not extend past the natural base or leave tissue uncovered. A base that is too wide may cause problems at the sides of the breast or under the arm.

Profile or projection

Profile describes how far the implant projects forward. Manufacturers use terms such as low, moderate, moderate-plus and high, but these names differ between brands and are not standard.

  • Lower projection gives a broader, more gradual look.
  • Higher projection gives a fuller, more forward look on a narrower base.

How they interact

For a given volume, a higher-profile implant has a narrower base. For a given base, a higher volume usually means more projection. A wide implant on a narrow chest can create problems, high-projection implants may look more obviously augmented in some people, and overly large dimensions raise the chance of stretching, thinning and later surgery.

Reading the surgical plan

A written plan should state the implant volume, base width, profile, surface, shape and placement, and explain why those choices suit your measurements. If two plans give the same volume but different widths, the look and the risks are not the same. Ask which measurement drove the decision.

Why cup size is a poor guide

Cup size depends on band size and manufacturer, so it cannot describe an implant. A 300 cc implant may produce different cup sizes on two people. Use cup size to describe your goal, then let measurements guide the choice.

Tools and questions

Surgeons measure the breast base, assess tissue pinch and may use sizers. Treat computer simulations as a rough indicator only.

  • What base width and profile do you recommend for me?
  • How will this look compared with other options?
  • What are the trade-offs?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Ask about width and projection, not just cc or cup size. See choosing implant size and the breast implants guide.

pages.h1: Breast Implant Rippling and Visibility: Causes and Prevention
pages.seoTitle: Breast Implant Rippling and Visibility: Causes and Prevention | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Why some breast implants show visible rippling or edges, who is more likely to be affected and what can reduce the risk.
pages.bannerLead: Rippling means wave-like ridges or wrinkles that can be seen or felt at the edges of an implant. It is a recognised issue, not a sign that you did something wrong.
related: How the pocket affects coverage and visibility.

blocks.html:
Visible or palpable rippling is one of the more common cosmetic concerns after augmentation. It is more likely in some bodies and with some implant choices than others.

Why it happens

  • Thin tissue coverage: little natural breast tissue or fat over the implant.
  • Implant position: implants placed over the muscle tend to show more.
  • Implant type: saline implants are generally more prone than cohesive silicone gel, though not exclusively.
  • Underfilling: a saline implant filled below its recommended volume can fold.
  • Size: an implant that is large relative to your tissue.
  • Weight loss or ageing: reducing the cover over time.

Where it shows

Rippling is most often noticed on the sides and lower part of the breast, and when leaning forward or standing. It may be felt rather than seen.

Reducing the risk

  • Choose an implant volume that suits your tissue.
  • Discuss placement under the muscle if you have little coverage; see implant placement.
  • Talk about the pros and cons of saline versus silicone for you.
  • Consider adding fat transfer on top of the implant in selected cases, as some surgeons do.
  • Maintain a stable weight.

If you are very lean or have little breast tissue, discuss whether implants are the right option at all. Fat transfer or a different approach may be more suitable in selected cases.

When rippling needs medical review

Rippling alone is usually cosmetic, but a new ridge with pain, a change in shape or a lump should be assessed. If the implant feels different or the breast becomes firm, your surgeon may check for rupture or capsular contracture. Do not assume every new change is rippling.

What if it develops?

Mild rippling may be acceptable. If it bothers you, options include changing the implant, adjusting placement or adding soft-tissue cover. Each has trade-offs and should be discussed with a surgeon. See breast revision. Revision is not guaranteed to remove rippling completely, especially if your tissue is thin, so ask what improvement is realistic before agreeing to another operation.

Questions to ask

  • How likely is visible rippling in someone with my tissue?
  • Which choice reduces it for me?
  • What would you do if it occurs?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Honest assessment of your tissue before surgery is the best protection against visible implants. See the breast implants guide.

pages.h1: Smooth vs Textured Breast Implants: Why Surface Matters
pages.seoTitle: Smooth vs Textured Breast Implants: Why Surface Matters | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: How smooth and textured implant surfaces differ, why texture became a safety issue and what to ask about the surface of any implant.
pages.bannerLead: The outer surface of an implant is a design feature that affects how it sits and how the body responds. It is also a safety question.
related: The lymphoma linked mainly to textured implants.
The wider guide to implant choices.

blocks.html:
Smooth and textured implants differ in more than feel. Surface design affects movement, the shapes available and, for some textures, the risk of a rare implant-associated lymphoma.

Smooth implants

The shell has a uniform, smooth surface. Smooth implants can move slightly within the pocket and are generally round. They have a long history of use.

Textured implants

The shell has a roughened surface. Texture was developed to help implants stay in place and to lower the chance of capsular contracture, particularly for shaped implants. Texturing varies widely, from fine to coarse (macro-textured).

The safety concern

A rare lymphoma, BIA-ALCL, has been linked mostly to textured implants, especially those with coarser texture. Some regulators asked for particular textured implants to be withdrawn, and several countries now restrict them. Read more on BIA-ALCL and implant illness.

blocks.heading: Trade-offs at a glance
head: Consideration
Smooth
Textured
rows: Can move more within the pocket
blocks.note: Individual risk depends on the exact implant, texture type and follow-up. Ask for the manufacturer and model.

blocks.html:
Texture and capsular contracture

Textured surfaces were introduced partly to reduce capsular contracture, but the evidence is not clear enough to say that texture is safer overall. Any benefit must be weighed against the lymphoma association and the availability of the exact implant. Ask for data specific to the model, not a general claim about “textured implants”.

What to ask

  • What is the exact surface of the implant you propose?
  • Has this implant been restricted or withdrawn anywhere?
  • Why do you recommend this surface for me?
  • What follow-up do you suggest for it?

If you are choosing between two implants and the only difference is surface, ask what the evidence is for that exact model and whether the same shape is available with a smooth surface.

If you already have textured implants

Do not panic. The risk of BIA-ALCL is low. Know what you have by checking your implant card, and report new swelling, a lump or pain to a doctor promptly. If you are unsure what you have, your implant card or operative record should identify the surface. If those records are missing, contact the clinic that performed the surgery.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Always ask what the surface is, and why it was chosen. See breast implant safety.

pages.h1: Implant Cards, Registries, Recalls and Warranties
pages.seoTitle: Implant Cards, Registries, Recalls and Warranties | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Why you should keep your implant card, how registries and recalls work, and what implant warranties usually cover.
pages.bannerLead: The paperwork around implants matters long after surgery. It identifies the device and supports follow-up, safety notices and warranty claims.
related: The wider guide to implant choice and follow-up.
What regulators and follow-up guidance say.

blocks.html:
The implant card is a medical record, not a receipt. Keep it with your other health documents and store a photograph of it somewhere you can find later.

The implant card

You should receive a card or record listing the manufacturer, model, size, surface, serial or batch numbers and the surgery date. Ask for it if it is not offered.

Why it matters

  • It identifies your implants if a safety notice is issued.
  • It helps future surgeons and radiology teams.
  • It supports claims under a warranty.

Registries

Several countries run breast implant registries that record implants and outcomes to monitor safety. Ask the clinic whether your details will be recorded in any applicable registry, how long the records are kept and who holds them. Registry availability and participation can change, so do not assume that a national system is in place.

If you move or change doctors

Give your new doctor a copy of your implant card and operative notes at your first visit. If you cannot find them, ask the original clinic or hospital for the records. This is especially important before imaging, pregnancy or any further breast surgery.

Recalls and safety notices

Regulators and manufacturers can issue notices when a problem is found. You may hear about them through the news, your clinic or the regulator. If you have a notice that matches your implant, contact your surgeon or doctor. A recall does not always mean the implant must be removed. It may recommend monitoring, or removal only if there is a rupture or symptoms. Follow the specific notice and your surgeon’s advice.

Warranties

Manufacturers may offer limited warranties for device failure. Typical features include:

  • They cover the implant, often not the cost of surgery or hospital fees.
  • They have time limits and conditions, such as registration.
  • Some clinics offer their own aftercare plans.

Read the terms before surgery, and ask what happens if the implant fails within the warranty period. Keep the surgery date, registration confirmation and any claim paperwork with your implant card.

Questions to ask

  • Will I get an implant card, and when?
  • What does the warranty cover and exclude?
  • If there is a recall, how will you contact me?
  • Where are my records stored, and for how long?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Treat the implant card like an important medical document. See the breast implants guide.

pages.h1: Breast Implant Risks: An Overview of What Can Go Wrong
pages.seoTitle: Breast Implant Risks: An Overview of What Can Go Wrong | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: A balanced overview of the main risks of breast implant surgery, from early complications to long-term issues, and why informed consent matters.
pages.bannerLead: All surgery has risks. Implants add device-related risks that can appear soon after surgery or years later.
related: The parent guide to rupture, contracture, ALCL and monitoring.
Candidacy, warning signs and choosing a surgeon.

blocks.html:
A risk list is not a prediction. It is the set of possibilities you should understand before consenting, together with how likely they are, how they are treated and who pays for further care.

Risks of any surgery

  • Bleeding, infection and wound-healing problems.
  • Reactions to anaesthesia.
  • Blood clots.
  • Scarring, which can be wide, raised or discoloured.

Risks specific to implants

  • Capsular contracture, where scar tissue tightens around the implant.
  • Implant rupture or leakage.
  • Displacement, rotation or visible rippling.
  • Changes in nipple or breast sensation.
  • Asymmetry or an unsatisfactory appearance.
  • Fluid collection (seroma) and haematoma.
  • Difficulty with breastfeeding in some cases.
  • Interference with breast imaging.
  • Rare serious conditions such as BIA-ALCL.
  • The chance of further surgery.

Risk is not the same for everyone

Smoking, existing conditions, implant type, size and surgical technique can all affect risk. Ask your surgeon to explain what applies to you rather than quoting a general figure.

How complications are managed

Most complications have a management pathway: antibiotics or drainage for infection, surgery for a large haematoma, capsule surgery for contracture, and removal or replacement for rupture. Ask who would manage each problem, where, and at what cost. A plan that describes only the operation but not the aftercare is incomplete.

Reading risk figures

Be careful with percentages: they depend on the study, the implant, how long people were followed and how a complication was defined. A single figure cannot describe your risk. Ask where the numbers come from, and ask what happens if the complication occurs.

Second opinions and cooling off

You do not have to decide at the first consultation. A cooling-off period gives you time to check the surgeon, the facility and the implant. If a clinic discourages this, treat that as a warning sign.

Informed consent

A proper consent process means you receive written information, the surgeon explains benefits, risks and alternatives, you have time to reflect and ask questions, and you can say no at any point.

Questions to ask

  • What are the most likely complications for me?
  • How are they treated, and who covers the cost?
  • What would make you advise against surgery for me?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A clinic that welcomes tough questions about risk is a good sign. See the breast implant safety guide.

pages.h1: Breast Implant Rupture: Silent and Visible
pages.seoTitle: Breast Implant Rupture: Silent and Visible | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: How breast implants can rupture or leak, why silicone ruptures may go unnoticed, how they are detected and what happens next.
pages.bannerLead: Implant shells can wear, tear or leak. Saline rupture is usually obvious; a silicone rupture may cause no symptoms at all.
related: Why implants are not lifetime devices.

blocks.html:
Rupture means the implant shell has failed. It can happen with any implant, at any time, and sometimes without an obvious cause.

What can cause it

  • Ageing and wear of the shell over time.
  • Surgical damage during insertion.
  • Injury or heavy compression.
  • Manufacturing defect, in rare cases.
  • Mammogram compression, rarely.

Some ruptures are found during imaging for another reason and may have been present for some time. This is why scheduled monitoring is useful even when you feel well.

Saline implants

If a saline implant leaks, it usually deflates over hours to days. The breast visibly shrinks and the body absorbs the salt water safely. The implant then needs replacing or removal.

Silicone gel implants

The gel is cohesive and often stays within the scar capsule, so there may be no visible change. This is called a silent rupture. Symptoms, when present, can include changes in shape or size, firmness, pain, tingling or a lump.

How it is detected

MRI is generally the most sensitive test. Ultrasound is often used as a first test, depending on availability and skill. Clinical examination alone can miss a rupture. The US FDA recommends imaging for silicone gel implants starting five to six years after surgery and then every two to three years; ask your surgeon what follow-up applies to you.

What imaging reports may say

A report may describe an intact implant, a suspected intracapsular rupture, an extracapsular rupture or indeterminate findings. The words matter, but they are not a treatment plan. Ask your surgeon to explain what the finding means for you and whether further imaging is needed.

What happens if rupture is found

Implants are usually removed or replaced, sometimes with removal of the surrounding capsule. The urgency depends on the implant type, symptoms and findings, so seek advice promptly rather than waiting for a routine appointment. An intact capsule with no symptoms may allow time to plan, while gel outside the capsule or symptoms usually prompts earlier surgery.

What to do

  • Report any new change in breast shape, size or comfort.
  • Keep regular check-ups.
  • Keep your implant records.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A silicone rupture can happen without symptoms, so scheduled monitoring matters. See how long implants last and breast implant safety.

pages.h1: Changes in Nipple and Breast Sensation After Augmentation
pages.seoTitle: Nipple and Breast Sensation Changes After Augmentation | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Why feeling in the nipple and breast can change after implant surgery, how common it is, how long it lasts and when to seek advice.
pages.bannerLead: Changes in sensation are among the most common effects of breast augmentation. Many are temporary, but some persist.
related: How the surgical route can affect sensation.
When numbness or pain needs urgent review.

blocks.html:
Nerves supply the nipple and breast through the tissue a surgeon works in. Even careful surgery can stretch, bruise or divide small nerves, and swelling can press on them.

What people report

  • Reduced or lost sensation.
  • Increased sensitivity or discomfort to touch.
  • Tingling, numbness or burning.
  • Changes in nipple sensitivity.

Factors that may influence it

  • Incision location, with some evidence linking the periareolar approach to a higher chance of nipple changes.
  • Implant size, since larger implants stretch tissue more.
  • Placement and surgical technique.
  • Existing nerve problems.

Sensation and breastfeeding

Nipple sensation and milk flow are related but not the same. Some people breastfeed successfully after augmentation, while others have difficulty, especially after periareolar incisions or revision surgery. If breastfeeding matters to you, raise it before surgery rather than assuming it will be unaffected. There is no technique that guarantees normal sensation; surgeons can try to avoid major nerves, but small branches vary between people and cannot always be seen.

How long does it last?

Often sensation returns gradually over weeks to months as swelling settles and nerves recover. In some people, changes last longer or are permanent. The outcome is not predictable, and no surgeon can guarantee normal sensation.

Some people notice numbness or tingling before the breast looks fully healed, while others notice a change only when sensation begins to return. Both patterns can occur. A review is worthwhile if the change is one-sided, painful or accompanied by skin colour change.

What you can do

  • Ask about the risk before surgery and include it in your consent discussion.
  • Protect numb areas from heat and injury, such as hot water bottles.
  • Report severe or worsening pain, or new numbness, to your surgeon.
  • Be patient, because recovery can take many months.

Documenting changes

Note when a change started, whether it is constant or intermittent, and whether it affects one or both sides. This helps your surgeon assess whether the cause is swelling, nerve irritation or something else. Bring the notes to your review rather than relying on memory.

When to seek advice

Sudden severe pain, loss of sensation with skin colour change, or signs of infection need prompt assessment. Do not wait for a routine follow-up if you are worried.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Sensation change is a real possibility. Make sure it is part of your informed consent. See breast augmentation incision options.

pages.h1: Early Complications: Infection, Haematoma and Seroma
pages.seoTitle: Early Implant Complications: Infection, Haematoma and Seroma | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Understand infection, bleeding (haematoma) and fluid collection (seroma) after breast implant surgery, including warning signs and treatment.
pages.bannerLead: Most early problems appear in the first days or weeks. Knowing the signs helps you act quickly rather than waiting to see whether they settle.
related: The wider guide to implant risks and monitoring.
When to call your team or seek emergency care.
Why late fluid collection needs assessment.

blocks.html:
Infection, bleeding and fluid collection are the early complications most worth recognising. Prompt treatment usually gives the best chance of resolving them.

Infection

Bacteria can enter the wound or implant pocket. Signs include fever, spreading redness, warmth, increasing pain, swelling and discharge. Treatment may include antibiotics, drainage and, in some cases, removal of the implant so the infection can clear. Surgeons use sterile techniques and sometimes antibiotics to lower the risk.

Haematoma

A haematoma is a collection of blood around the implant. It usually occurs soon after surgery and causes rapid, often one-sided swelling, tightness and pain. Small ones may settle. Larger ones often need a return to theatre to drain the blood and control bleeding. Blood thinners, certain supplements and high blood pressure can raise the risk.

Seroma

A seroma is a build-up of fluid. Early seromas may settle or be drained. Fluid that appears long after surgery, especially more than a year later, needs prompt medical assessment, because it can occasionally signal BIA-ALCL. Do not ignore it. See BIA-ALCL and implant illness.

Red flags that need urgent care

Seek emergency care for difficulty breathing, chest pain, fainting, a rapid painful swelling of one breast, or skin that turns pale, blue or blistered. These can signal a clot, major bleeding or poor blood supply. Do not wait for a routine appointment.

Other early problems

  • Wound-edge breakdown or delayed healing.
  • Skin or nipple colour change, which may signal poor blood supply.
  • Implant malposition.

Why follow-up matters

Some problems are easier to treat when found early. Keep your review appointments even if you feel well, and tell the team about any change in comfort, shape or wound healing. A photograph taken at the same angle can help you describe a change.

What to do

  • Know your surgeon’s emergency contact before you leave.
  • Report symptoms early rather than waiting.
  • Go to emergency care if you cannot reach the team.

Do not try to drain a wound or collection yourself, and do not start leftover antibiotics without advice.

Questions to ask

  • How do you lower the risk of infection and bleeding?
  • What would trigger a return to theatre?
  • Who covers the costs if I need further surgery for a complication?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Early recognition and treatment usually leads to better outcomes. See the full list of warning signs after breast surgery.

pages.h1: Who Should Delay or Avoid Breast Implants?
pages.cardTitle: Who should delay or avoid implants
pages.seoTitle: Who Should Delay or Avoid Breast Implants? | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Situations in which breast implants may be unsuitable or better delayed, including health, lifestyle and expectation-related factors.
pages.bannerLead: Breast implants are not right for everyone, or not right at every time. A responsible surgeon will say honestly if it is better to wait or choose another path.
related: What a surgeon assesses before surgery.
How to prepare for an honest discussion.

blocks.html:
A surgeon who turns some people down, or asks them to wait, is protecting them. Being told “not yet” is not a judgment about how much you deserve care.

Reasons to delay

  • Pregnancy or breastfeeding.
  • Active infection anywhere in the body, especially in or near the breast.
  • Recent significant weight change or plans to lose weight, since results may change.
  • Smoking or nicotine use, which slows healing and raises complications.
  • Plans for pregnancy soon, which some surgeons advise waiting for.
  • An unassessed breast lump or abnormal screening result.

Reasons implants may be unsuitable

  • Poorly controlled medical conditions or bleeding disorders.
  • Conditions that significantly affect healing.
  • Previous radiotherapy to the chest, which can raise complication rates and calls for specialist advice.
  • Very thin tissue where an implant could not be adequately covered.
  • A strong preference to avoid any future surgery, since implants may need it.

Autoimmune and other conditions

People with autoimmune or connective-tissue conditions should discuss this with their specialist and surgeon. Evidence is limited and individual advice is essential.

Psychological factors

Some people have intense distress about their appearance that does not match how others see them, as in body dysmorphic disorder. Surgery generally does not relieve this and can make things worse. A responsible surgeon may suggest talking to a mental health professional first. This is a sign of care, not rejection.

Unrealistic expectations

Surgery cannot change life circumstances, guarantee a relationship or career outcome, or produce an exact result seen in a photograph.

Questions for a second opinion

Ask whether the surgeon would recommend the same operation for a family member, what they would do differently if you had more or less tissue, and what they would advise if you wanted to wait a year. A consistent, reasoned answer is more reassuring than a sales pitch.

Alternatives

In some cases a different option, such as a breast lift, fat transfer, a supportive bra or no procedure, may fit better.

Questions to ask

  • Are there reasons I should wait or avoid implants?
  • What would improve my suitability?
  • What alternatives do you suggest?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Good surgeons turn some people down or ask them to wait. That is protective, not obstructive. See breast enlargement safety.

pages.h1: Is Fat Transfer Right for You? Candidacy and Limits
pages.seoTitle: Fat Transfer Breast Augmentation: Candidacy and Limits | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Who may be suited to breast fat transfer, who may not, and why donor fat, skin and goals matter.
pages.bannerLead: Fat transfer can add modest volume using your own tissue, but it is not suitable for every goal or body type.
related: The parent guide to the procedure, recovery and risks.
Why retention varies and what it means for your result.
When the two approaches are used together.

blocks.html:
Fat transfer uses your own fat to add volume. It suits some goals well and others poorly. The main limits are how much donor fat you have, how much space your breast tissue can accept, and how much change you want.

Who it may suit

  • People who want a modest, natural-feeling increase in size
  • Those with enough fat in areas such as the abdomen, thighs or flanks to harvest
  • People who prefer to avoid a manufactured device in the body
  • Those correcting small contour irregularities or mild asymmetry
  • Selected people in reconstruction, under specialist care

Who may find it unsuitable

  • Very slim people with little donor fat
  • Those wanting a large increase in size in one operation
  • People with tight breast skin, which limits how much fat can safely be placed
  • Smokers, because blood supply affects fat survival
  • People with conditions that raise surgical or anaesthetic risk
  • Anyone who expects the full injected volume to remain

Why skin and tissue matter

Injected fat needs space and a blood supply. Tight skin, scarred tissue or a small breast envelope restricts how much can be placed and may reduce how much survives. This is why the same volume can produce different results in different people.

Realistic goals

A typical goal is a subtle change rather than a dramatic one. Some people need more than one session, and not everyone is pleased with the final volume. An implant may be more predictable for a larger increase. Read how much fat survives before setting expectations.

Timing

Surgeons usually prefer a stable weight before fat transfer, because later weight change alters both donor areas and breast volume. If pregnancy is part of your near-term plans, discuss whether waiting would be more predictable.

What assessment involves

The surgeon examines your breasts and donor areas, reviews your health and smoking history, and discusses what is realistic. Photographs and, in some cases, breast imaging may be arranged. No surgeon can guarantee a specific cup size or retention rate.

Questions to ask

  • Do I have enough donor fat?
  • How much increase is realistic for me?
  • Might an implant suit my goals better?
  • Who will perform the liposuction and injection?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Fat transfer works best for modest change in people with adequate donor fat and healthy tissue. It is not a reliable way to achieve a large increase in one operation.

pages.h1: How Breast Fat Transfer Is Performed
pages.seoTitle: How Breast Fat Transfer Is Performed | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: A step-by-step explanation of fat harvesting, processing and injection in breast fat transfer, with what to ask a surgeon.
pages.bannerLead: Fat transfer has three main stages: harvesting, processing and injection. The details vary between surgeons and can affect the result.
related: The parent guide to candidacy, recovery and risks.
Is fat transfer right for you?
Donor fat, skin and realistic goals.
What to expect at the breast and donor sites.

blocks.html:
Fat transfer has three main stages: harvesting, processing and injection. Surgeons differ in technique, and there is no single method that has been proven best for every patient.

1. Planning

The surgeon examines your breasts and donor areas, discusses your goals and marks the areas to be treated. Photographs are usually taken for your records. The plan should include how much fat is likely to be needed and whether one session is realistic.

2. Harvesting

Fat is collected by liposuction through small incisions, often under general anaesthesia, though some cases use sedation or local anaesthesia. The surgeon uses gentle techniques intended to protect the fat cells. Common donor areas are the abdomen, flanks and thighs.

3. Processing

The harvested fat is prepared by methods such as washing, filtering or centrifuging to separate usable fat from fluid, oil and debris. There is no single agreed method, and evidence on which is best is still developing.

4. Injection

The fat is injected in many small amounts through tiny entry points, at different depths in the breast. Spreading small amounts helps each deposit get a blood supply. Overfilling can reduce survival and raise complications.

5. Dressings

The small wounds are covered and a supportive garment may be advised for the donor areas. Avoid pressure on the breasts as directed, because compression may affect the transferred fat.

Time and setting

The operation commonly takes a few hours, depending on the extent of liposuction and treatment. It is usually done in a hospital or accredited facility by a surgeon with experience in both liposuction and breast surgery.

Some surgeons use pre-expansion

A suction device worn before surgery is used by some surgeons to prepare the breast tissue. Evidence and experience vary, so ask whether it is advised for you and what it adds.

Scars and donor sites

Liposuction entry points and breast injection sites leave small scars. Donor-site bruising and contour changes may take weeks to settle, and the amount of fat removed affects recovery.

Questions to ask

  • Where will you take fat from, and how much?
  • How do you process and inject it?
  • What anaesthesia will be used, and by whom?
  • How many sessions might be needed?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: The technique matters, so ask your surgeon to explain their method, their experience and why it suits your goals.

pages.h1: Recovery After Breast Fat Transfer
pages.seoTitle: Recovery After Breast Fat Transfer | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: What to expect after breast fat transfer, including swelling, donor-site recovery, garments, activity limits and when to call your surgeon.
pages.bannerLead: Recovery involves two areas: the breasts that received fat and the donor areas where fat was taken. Follow your own surgeon’s instructions.
related: The parent guide to candidacy, technique and risks.
Fat necrosis, oil cysts and calcifications.
Symptoms that need urgent medical attention.

blocks.html:
Recovery involves two areas: the breasts that received fat and the donor areas where fat was taken. Follow your surgeon’s instructions, which may differ from this general guide.

The first days

  • Soreness, swelling and bruising in the breasts and donor sites
  • Fluid leakage from small incisions
  • Tightness from compression garments
  • Tiredness after anaesthesia

Donor-site bruising can feel more uncomfortable than the breasts, especially if a larger area was treated.

Garments

You may be asked to wear a compression garment on the donor areas. For the breasts, some surgeons advise avoiding tight bras or pressure for a period, because compression may harm the transferred fat. Follow the specific advice you receive.

Activity

Light walking is generally encouraged to support circulation. Strenuous exercise, heavy lifting and sleeping on your front are usually restricted for a time, which your surgeon will specify. Avoid massage unless advised.

Swelling and change in size

The breasts look largest early on because of swelling. As swelling settles and some fat is reabsorbed over the following weeks and months, size may reduce. A final assessment is usually made after several months, not in the first few weeks.

Avoid

  • Smoking and nicotine, which can impair healing and fat survival
  • Dramatic weight loss, which can reduce results
  • Unsupervised massage or devices

Call your surgeon if you have

Fever, spreading redness, severe or increasing pain, pus, rapidly increasing swelling or skin colour change. See our warning signs page and seek urgent care if symptoms are severe.

Returning to work

Desk work may be possible within days to a week or two, depending on comfort and the extent of liposuction. Physical work, lifting and exercise usually take longer. Ask for a written plan rather than relying on a general timeline.

Driving

Do not drive while you are taking strong pain relief or cannot move comfortably and react safely. Check your surgeon’s advice and your insurance conditions.

Follow-up

Expect check-ups, photographs and advice about breast imaging. Tell any imaging team that you have had fat transfer, because the changes can affect how scans are read.

Follow-up and records

At each review, ask what change is expected, which symptoms need a call and when you can return to each activity. Keep the operation note and tell future clinicians about the transfer. That history can help a radiologist interpret later imaging, but it does not replace routine breast screening or assessment of a new symptom.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Patience matters, because the early look is not the final result. Most of the settling takes weeks to months, not days.

pages.h1: Lumps After Fat Transfer: Fat Necrosis, Oil Cysts and Calcifications
pages.seoTitle: Lumps After Fat Transfer: Fat Necrosis and Oil Cysts | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Why lumps can form after breast fat transfer, how they are assessed and why any new breast lump should still be checked by a doctor.
pages.bannerLead: After fat transfer, some people notice firm areas or lumps. Many are harmless, but every new lump should be assessed.
related: The parent guide to the procedure and recovery.
Assessment, warning signs and choosing a surgeon.
When a symptom needs urgent attention.

blocks.html:
After fat transfer, some people notice firm areas or lumps. Many are harmless, but every new lump should be assessed rather than assumed to be a normal effect of surgery.

Fat necrosis

Fat necrosis happens when injected fat does not get enough blood supply and its cells die. This can form firm, sometimes tender lumps. It is a recognised complication of fat grafting, not evidence that the procedure has failed.

Oil cysts

As fat breaks down, it can leave fluid-filled pockets called oil cysts. They may feel like smooth, soft or firm lumps and can change over time.

Calcifications

Over time, areas of damaged fat can harden with calcium deposits. These may show on mammograms. Radiologists can often tell benign patterns from concerning ones, but sometimes further tests are needed.

How common is it?

Frequency varies with technique, the volume injected and individual factors. Ask your surgeon about their own rates and how they manage these problems.

Why assessment matters

A lump after fat transfer is not automatically fat necrosis. It can also be something unrelated, including breast cancer. A clinician may use examination, ultrasound, mammography, MRI or biopsy to find out.

What a lump may feel like

Fat necrosis can feel firm, irregular or tender; an oil cyst may feel smooth and round. These descriptions overlap with other breast conditions, so how a lump feels cannot confirm the cause.

Imaging after fat transfer

Mammograms and ultrasound may show calcifications or cysts related to the graft. Radiologists compare the pattern with your surgical history, which is why accurate records and a clear explanation of the procedure are useful.

What to do

  • Do not assume a lump is harmless
  • Report new lumps, hardness or skin change promptly
  • Tell imaging teams about your fat transfer
  • Keep records of your procedure and any imaging

Treatment

Many areas need only monitoring. Painful or concerning lumps may be aspirated or removed. Treatment depends on the diagnosis, not on the appearance alone.

Reducing risk

Surgeons aim to inject small amounts in several layers and avoid overfilling. No technique removes the risk entirely.

Do not wait for a scheduled check

Contact a clinician promptly for a rapidly enlarging area, significant redness, fever, discharge, a marked skin change or pain that is getting worse. A new breast or armpit lump deserves assessment even years after transfer, whether or not you recently had imaging.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Lumps after fat transfer are a known issue, but they should always be checked. See Breast Enlargement Safety.

pages.h1: Combining Fat Transfer With Implants
pages.seoTitle: Combining Fat Transfer With Breast Implants | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: When surgeons combine fat transfer with breast implants, the possible benefits, limits and questions to ask about this composite approach.
pages.bannerLead: Some surgeons use a small amount of fat together with an implant, sometimes called composite augmentation. It adds complexity as well as potential benefits.
related: The parent guide to fat transfer.
Compare volume, recovery, scarring and longevity.
Monitoring and possible replacement over time.

blocks.html:
Some surgeons use a small amount of fat together with an implant, sometimes called composite augmentation. The aim is usually to improve soft-tissue cover or contour rather than to add most of the volume.

Why combine them?

  • To add soft-tissue cover over an implant and soften visible edges or rippling
  • To improve cleavage or the upper-breast contour
  • To correct small irregularities or asymmetry
  • To refine results after earlier surgery

Who may be considered

People with thin tissue who want an implant but are concerned about visibility, and those needing contour correction. Donor fat must be available, and the breast must have enough room for both the implant and the graft.

Staged or combined?

Some surgeons perform liposuction and implant placement in one operation, while others stage the procedures to limit operating time or to see how tissues settle. There is no single correct schedule; your anatomy, health and the reason for combining the procedures should guide the plan.

What fat can and cannot add

Fat is best used for contour and soft-tissue cover. It should not be presented as a way to make a large, predictable size increase, because retention varies. Ask how much of the planned result depends on the implant and how much on the graft.

Trade-offs

  • Two procedures in one: liposuction plus implant surgery
  • Longer operation and recovery
  • Some of the fat may be reabsorbed
  • Risks of both, including lumps from fat necrosis and implant-related complications
  • Greater cost and need for follow-up

Imaging considerations

Both implants and transferred fat can affect breast imaging. Tell radiology teams about both, and keep a record of the implant details and the transfer.

Evidence

Results are reported by surgeons and in studies, but long-term comparative data are still limited. Ask for the evidence your surgeon relies on and how they judge success.

Plan each component separately

A sound consultation identifies what the implant is meant to achieve and what the graft is meant to achieve. It should also cover the liposuction sites, incision scars, recovery demands and future monitoring. “Composite” is a description of two procedures, not a benefit in itself.

Questions to ask

  • What would fat add to my implant result?
  • How many cases like mine have you done?
  • What extra risks apply?
  • What happens to the fat if I later change the implant?

pages.h1: Understanding Breast Sagging: Types and What a Lift Can Do
pages.seoTitle: Types of Breast Sagging and What a Lift Can Do | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: How surgeons classify breast sagging (ptosis), the difference between true sagging and pseudoptosis, and what a lift can and cannot change.
pages.bannerLead: The right procedure depends on how much skin and tissue has descended, not just on breast size.
related: The parent guide to techniques, scars and longevity.
When volume, position or both need to change.
How the scar pattern follows the lift required.

blocks.html:
Breast sagging, or ptosis, happens when skin stretches and breast tissue descends. Causes include ageing, pregnancy, breastfeeding, weight change, gravity and genetics.

Classifying ptosis

Surgeons often assess the nipple position compared with the fold beneath the breast. A commonly used scale describes:

  • Grade 1 (mild): nipple at the level of the fold
  • Grade 2 (moderate): nipple below the fold but above the lowest point of the breast
  • Grade 3 (severe): nipple at or below the lowest point, pointing downward
  • Pseudoptosis: the breast hangs below the fold but the nipple stays above it

Why classification matters

It helps decide whether a lift is needed, which technique suits, and whether an implant could be enough on its own. Two people with the same cup size can need very different operations.

How the assessment is made

The surgeon observes the breast from the front and side, measures nipple position relative to the fold, and considers skin elasticity, breast volume and asymmetry. Photographs may help track change, but they do not replace an in-person examination.

Skin quality and volume

Sagging is not only about loose skin. A breast with little tissue may need volume as well as lifting, while a heavy breast may need reduction rather than augmentation. The plan should address both shape and weight.

A measurement is only one part of the decision

Ptosis grades describe nipple position, but they do not capture skin quality, breast width, tissue weight, bra fit or how you feel about your shape. They are a planning tool, not a score that proves someone needs surgery or needs it quickly.

What a lift does

A breast lift removes excess skin, reshapes tissue and raises the nipple to a higher position. It may also reduce a stretched areola. See Breast Lift Surgery.

What it does not do

  • It does not add much volume
  • It does not stop future ageing or gravity
  • It does not leave you without scars
  • It does not guarantee a particular shape

If you also want more fullness

A lift can be combined with an implant or fat transfer, or staged. See our page on lift vs augmentation.

Questions to ask

  • What grade of sagging do I have?
  • Do I need a lift, an implant, or both?
  • What scars does my case need?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: The right procedure depends on how much skin and tissue has descended, not just on size.

pages.h1: Breast Lift Incisions and Scars: What to Expect
pages.seoTitle: Breast Lift Incisions and Scars: What to Expect | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: The main breast lift incision patterns, which sagging each suits, how scars heal and how to look after them.
pages.bannerLead: The amount of sagging largely decides the scar pattern. More lift usually means more scar.
related: The parent guide to shape, longevity and recovery.
Scarring, nipple blood supply and sensation changes.
General scar-care guidance after breast surgery.

blocks.html:
The amount of sagging largely decides the scar pattern. More lift usually means more scar, and every lift leaves permanent marks.

Periareolar (around the areola)

A scar encircles the areola. It suits mild sagging and may reshape the areola. Scars can widen in some people, and flattening of the breast is a known concern with this technique alone.

Vertical (lollipop)

A scar goes around the areola and straight down to the breast fold. It suits moderate sagging and offers more reshaping than an areolar-only lift.

Inverted T (anchor)

In addition, a scar runs along the fold. It suits significant sagging or large amounts of excess skin and gives the most control. This is the longest scar.

How scars mature

Scars usually look red or raised at first, then flatten and fade over a year or longer. Some people develop widened, thick (hypertrophic) or keloid scars. Healing is partly genetic.

Looking after scars

  • Follow wound-care instructions
  • Avoid tension, heavy lifting and sun exposure on healing scars
  • Do not use scar products or silicone sheets unless your surgeon advises
  • Report wounds that open, discharge or look infected

Scar revision

If a scar widens, thickens or causes tension, a surgeon may offer scar revision after the tissues have settled. This is another operation with its own healing and does not guarantee a fine scar. Some scars are better managed with time and non-surgical care.

Plan for scars before surgery

Ask the surgeon to show where each incision will sit in relation to your usual bra or swimwear. Scar lines can be uneven and may not be completely hidden by every garment. A good consent discussion explains the likely trade-off before, rather than after, surgery.

Nipple sensation and position

Moving the nipple can change sensation, and the final position may differ slightly from the planned mark as swelling resolves. Discuss both before surgery rather than judging the early result.

Trade-off to weigh

Some people accept longer scars for a better shape; others prefer shorter scars with less lift. Be honest with your surgeon about how you feel, and ask to see typical healed scars with consent.

Questions to ask

  • Which pattern do you recommend, and why?
  • Where will each scar sit relative to my bra or swimwear?
  • Can I see typical healed scars, with permission, at one year?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Every lift trades scars for position and shape. Make sure you understand the trade-off before you consent.

pages.h1: Recovery After a Breast Lift
pages.seoTitle: Recovery After a Breast Lift | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: What to expect in the days and weeks after a breast lift, including dressings, activity limits, scar care and warning signs.
pages.bannerLead: Recovery varies with the extent of the lift and whether it is combined with other surgery. Your surgeon’s instructions take priority.
related: The parent guide to suitability, scars and longevity.
What can go wrong and how risk is reduced.
Symptoms that need urgent medical attention.

blocks.html:
Recovery varies with the extent of the lift and whether it is combined with other surgery. Your surgeon’s instructions take priority over any general timeline.

The first days

  • Soreness, swelling, bruising and tightness
  • Dressings and a surgical or support bra
  • Sometimes small drains, removed after a few days
  • Numbness or altered sensation around the breast and nipple

Most people go home the same day or after one night.

Pain and medicines

You will usually be given pain relief. Follow instructions and avoid medicines you were told to stop, since some raise bleeding risk.

Activity

  • Walk gently from early on, which helps circulation
  • Avoid lifting, pushing and strenuous exercise for several weeks, as advised
  • Avoid raising your arms above shoulder height if told to, since tension can stress wounds
  • Return to desk work after a period determined by your surgeon, and to heavier work later

Sleeping

Sleeping on your back with your upper body slightly raised is commonly advised. Avoid sleeping on your front.

Support garments

Wear the recommended bra as directed, usually for several weeks. Avoid underwired bras until your surgeon says it is safe.

Wound and scar care

Keep dressings clean and dry as instructed, and attend wound checks. Scars mature over a year or more. Protect them from the sun.

The shape will change

Swelling and tightness mean the breasts may look high and tight at first. They settle gradually over weeks to months.

Follow-up is part of recovery

Attend wound and scar checks even if you feel well. Ask when changes in shape, nipple sensation or scar colour are expected and when they are not. Take concerns to your own surgical team rather than changing dressings, bras or scar treatments based only on advice online.

Driving and work

Do not drive while taking strong pain relief or while movement is restricted. Desk work may be possible after a week or two, but physical work and exercise usually need longer. Ask for advice specific to your operation.

When swelling settles

Early swelling can make the breasts look high and tight. Most change occurs over the first few months, but subtle settling can continue for longer. Avoid judging the final shape in the first weeks.

Call your surgeon if you notice

Fever, increasing pain, spreading redness, a wound opening, rapid swelling on one side, or skin around the nipple turning dark or pale. See warning signs.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Plan for rest, help at home and patience while the shape settles. See Breast Lift Surgery.

pages.h1: Breast Lift Risks: What to Know Before You Decide
pages.seoTitle: Breast Lift Risks: Scars, Sensation and Healing | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: The main risks of breast lift surgery, including scarring, nipple blood supply, sensation changes, asymmetry and the chance of sagging again.
pages.bannerLead: A lift is a major operation on the breast’s blood supply and skin. Understanding the risks supports informed consent.
related: The parent guide to planning, scars and longevity.
Candidacy, warning signs and choosing a surgeon.

blocks.html:
A lift is a major operation on the breast’s blood supply and skin. Understanding the risks supports informed consent and realistic expectations.

General risks

  • Bleeding and haematoma
  • Infection
  • Reactions to anaesthesia
  • Blood clots
  • Delayed wound healing, especially at scar junctions

Risks specific to a lift

  • Scarring: visible, widened or thickened scars
  • Nipple and areola blood supply: because the nipple is moved, its blood supply can be compromised. Serious loss is uncommon, but it can occur, particularly in smokers or with large lifts
  • Sensation changes: reduced, lost or heightened nipple and breast sensation
  • Asymmetry: differences in shape, size or nipple position
  • Contour irregularities or fat necrosis lumps
  • Breastfeeding effects: many people can still breastfeed, but it is not guaranteed
  • Recurrent sagging: gravity and ageing continue to act
  • Need for revision

Factors that raise risk

  • Smoking
  • Large breasts or extensive lifts
  • Significant weight change
  • Conditions affecting healing, such as poorly controlled diabetes

Risk is personal, not a checklist score

A complication can be uncommon overall but still matter greatly to a particular person. Ask which risks are most relevant to your anatomy, medicines, smoking or nicotine use and planned operation, how they would be recognised, and what treatment or revision could involve.

Seroma and delayed healing

Fluid can collect under the skin (seroma), and small areas of the wound may heal slowly, especially where incisions meet. These problems are usually manageable with drainage, dressings or antibiotics, but they can prolong recovery and affect scarring.

Anaesthesia and general health

Anaesthetic risk depends on your health, medicines and history. A preoperative assessment may identify conditions that need treatment before surgery. Report sleep apnoea, bleeding disorders, previous clots and all supplements.

What to tell your surgeon

Be explicit about smoking, nicotine products, weight change and any plan for pregnancy. These factors affect tissue healing and the timing of surgery.

Combining with implants

Combining a lift with an implant increases complexity. Some surgeons stage the two operations for safety.

Reducing risk

  • Stop smoking well before surgery
  • Reach a stable weight
  • Follow aftercare instructions
  • Choose a surgeon who performs lifts regularly

Questions to ask

  • Which risks are most relevant for me?
  • How do you protect the nipple’s blood supply?
  • What is your approach if healing is delayed?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: The risks are manageable when you are well prepared, but they are real. Ask how your surgeon prevents, recognises and treats them.

pages.h1: Will a Breast Lift Last? Protecting Your Results
pages.seoTitle: How Long Does a Breast Lift Last? | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: How long breast lift results can last, what causes sagging to return and what you can do to look after your results.
pages.bannerLead: A lift repositions the breast but does not stop time. Results last for varying lengths, and some descent after surgery is normal.
related: The parent guide to technique, scars and recovery.
If a lift was combined with an implant.
How future pregnancy can affect breast shape.

blocks.html:
A lift repositions the breast but does not stop time. Results last for varying lengths, and some descent after surgery is normal.

Why sagging can return

  • Gravity and ageing reduce skin elasticity
  • Weight changes stretch skin again
  • Pregnancy and breastfeeding alter breast tissue
  • Hormones and menopause change breast density
  • Heavy breast tissue puts more strain on skin
  • Genetics affect how skin holds up

What is normal

Breasts typically settle in the first months after a lift, and some descent is expected. Long-term results vary widely, and no one can promise how many years it will last.

Protecting your result

  • Maintain a stable weight
  • Wear supportive bras, especially for exercise, as your surgeon advises
  • Avoid smoking, which affects skin quality
  • Protect your skin from the sun
  • Consider the timing of future pregnancies
  • Attend follow-ups

Weight and pregnancy timing

Large weight changes can stretch or shrink the breast and alter the result. If you are planning pregnancy, discuss timing with your surgeon. A lift does not prevent pregnancy or breastfeeding, but pregnancy can change shape and volume.

Posture and support

A well-fitting, supportive bra can reduce strain during exercise, but it cannot prevent natural ageing or guarantee that a particular bra will keep the result in place. There is no evidence that special creams or exercises preserve a lift.

A review does not always mean revision

Some settling, scar change and gradual descent are expected and may only need reassurance or observation. A sudden change, a new lump or persistent one-sided pain needs a diagnosis first. Do not assume that every change is cosmetic or that another operation is the only answer.

When to seek review

Ask for assessment if you notice a new lump, persistent pain, a change in one breast or a sudden loss of shape, rather than assuming it is expected settling.

What about implants?

An implant can add volume and upper fullness but adds weight, and does not stop ageing. Implants may also need replacing in time. See how long implants last.

If sagging returns

Options include observation, a repeat lift or other procedures. Revision surgery has its own risks and may be less predictable than the first operation.

Questions to ask

  • How long might my result last?
  • What can I do to protect it?
  • What if I plan pregnancy?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Think of a lift as resetting the clock, not stopping it. Stable weight and realistic expectations help protect the result.

pages.h1: Why People Need Breast Revision Surgery
pages.seoTitle: Why People Need Breast Revision Surgery | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: The most common reasons for breast revision surgery, including implant problems, shape changes and personal choice, and what revision involves.
pages.bannerLead: Revision surgery can address a device problem, a change in shape or a change in what someone wants. Needing it is common.
related: The parent guide to exchange, removal and repair.

blocks.html:
Breast revision surgery is any further operation to correct, replace or remove implants or improve an earlier result. There are many reasons, and needing revision is not a failure of the patient.

Medical or device-related reasons

  • Capsular contracture (see our implant safety page)
  • Implant rupture or deflation
  • Infection or an exposed implant
  • An implant recall or safety notice
  • Rare complications such as BIA-ALCL

Position and appearance reasons

  • An implant that has moved, tilted or is sitting too low or too high
  • Visible rippling or edges
  • Asymmetry
  • Dissatisfaction with size or shape
  • Scar problems

Life-stage reasons

  • Changes after pregnancy, breastfeeding, weight change or ageing
  • A wish to change size or shape
  • A wish to remove implants
  • Breast changes that need a lift

Revision is common

Many people with implants will have another operation at some point. This is not a failure of the patient. See how long implants last.

First steps

  • Get a clear diagnosis of what is wrong
  • Collect your implant card and surgery records
  • Consider imaging if rupture or contracture is suspected
  • Seek a surgeon with revision experience, and consider a second opinion

Not every concern needs an operation

Some concerns can be monitored, treated without surgery or addressed by changing support garments, pain management or expectations. A surgeon should explain why surgery is likely to help in your case, what it cannot correct and what observation would involve. A revision should not be presented as the only response to normal settling.

Urgency depends on symptoms

Severe pain, fever, spreading redness, sudden swelling, an enlarging breast, a new mass or a wound problem needs prompt medical advice. Other concerns, such as a stable position or size preference, can usually be assessed carefully over time. Do not delay urgent assessment while seeking cosmetic opinions.

Choosing the right team

Complex revision may need imaging specialists, an anaesthetist and a surgeon who regularly manages scar tissue, implant pockets and explant decisions. Ask who would coordinate your care and what happens if an unexpected finding changes the plan during surgery.

Realistic expectations

Revision can be more complex than first-time surgery because of scar tissue and altered anatomy. Outcomes and risks can differ, and more than one operation may be needed.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Needing revision is common, and the best start is a clear understanding of the cause.

pages.h1: Implant Removal and Exchange: Options and What to Expect
pages.seoTitle: Breast Implant Removal and Exchange | Quantum Health
pages.seoDescription: Compare removing implants, replacing them and removing them with a lift or fat transfer, including how breast shape may change.
pages.bannerLead: Someone with implants may choose to remove them, replace them or change them for another type. The right option depends on your reasons, tissue and goals.
related: The parent guide to planning revision.
Capsulotomy, capsulectomy and en bloc removal.
A lift may be combined with removal.

blocks.html:
Someone with implants may choose to remove them, replace them or change them for another type. The right option depends on your reasons, your tissue and your goals.

Removal only (explant)

Implants are taken out without replacement. The capsule may be left, partly removed or removed whole. Reasons include symptoms, complications, ageing implants or personal preference.

Exchange

Old implants are replaced with new ones, perhaps of a different size, type or position. Exchange may be combined with capsule surgery or a lift.

Removal with a lift

After removal, the breast skin may be loose, especially if the implants were large or have been in for years. A lift may be considered at the same time or later.

Removal with fat transfer

Some people choose fat transfer to restore some volume after implant removal. It is not suitable for everyone and may need more than one session.

How the breast may look afterwards

The shape after removal depends on your original breast, how long implants were in, tissue changes and skin quality. Expect possible loss of volume, laxity or contour irregularity. A surgeon can discuss likely outcomes, though they cannot be guaranteed.

Recovery

Removal is often shorter than the original surgery, but recovery depends on whether capsule surgery or a lift is done. Follow your surgeon’s instructions on garments, activity and wound care.

Decide what happens to the capsule

A capsule is scar tissue that normally forms around an implant. Whether it is left, released or removed depends on findings such as contracture, rupture, fluid, abnormal tissue and how safely it can be separated from the chest wall. Ask for the reason for the planned extent of surgery, not simply a label.

Think in stages when needed

If there is infection, uncertain tissue health or a major change in size, the safest plan may separate removal, healing and reconstruction. A staged plan can feel disappointing, but it may give tissue time to settle and make the next decision more reliable.

Planning

  • Ask about the likely look afterwards
  • Discuss the capsule and why it is or is not removed
  • Consider imaging and any need for pathology tests
  • Think about breast screening in future

If you have symptoms you attribute to implants, see a doctor to assess other possible causes. See BIA-ALCL and implant illness.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Plan for what the breast will look like after removal, not just the removal itself.
