  • It will reshape breasts to some extent and can also be used to correct unequal breast size.
  • Fat transfer (lipomodelling, lipofilling or fat grafting) is an alternative in a few people but is not suitable for all and often requires more than one episode of surgery.
  • Patients tend to be pleased with results, but you need realistic expectations and must understand what can and cannot be achieved, the limitations of surgery and the long-term consequences of implants.
  • Your initial consultation should be with the surgeon who will do the operation; your surgeon will normally seek permission to write to your GP; a consultation fee is normal.
  • At consultation you will be examined, measurements taken, and implant shapes, sizes and pocket positions discussed; some surgeons use implant sizers in a bra or 3D photography, which is only a guide — the same implant can look very different in different people.
  • You should be given a cooling-off period of at least two weeks before surgery and offered a second consultation; you should not feel rushed.
  • Breast augmentation is a lifetime commitment, not a one-stop permanent solution: you will need revision surgery as the years go by and must be prepared personally and financially.
  • Nobody needs an urgent breast augmentation — if you are not offered a cooling-off period or are put under pressure, walk away.
  • Surgeons should be listed on the GMC specialist register (gmc-uk.org); membership of ABS, BAAPS and/or BAPRAS indicates a standard set of recognised qualifications.
  • Internet search listings may be promotional; a prominent listing measures marketing ability, not service quality.
  • Cosmetic breast augmentation is not available on the NHS except in exceptional circumstances such as very uneven breasts, no breasts, or as part of reconstruction; after surgery abroad the NHS will only deal with emergency complications on return.
  • Breast enlargement involves placing an implant under the breast tissue; implants are usually inserted through an incision under the breast at the crease, but can also go in via the armpit or around the nipple.
  • Implants can sit behind the breast on top of the chest wall muscle (sub-glandular) or behind the breast and muscle (sub-muscular); your surgeon will advise which is appropriate.
  • Sub-glandular placement is considered the simplest enlargement procedure and less likely to cause significant discomfort; it is also effective with some drooping.
  • Sub-muscular placement provides more padding for the implant, helpful for slender patients and those with little breast tissue, reducing the chances of feeling or seeing the implant.
  • Dual plane augmentation combines the two routes, placing implants partly behind the breast and partly behind the muscle; implants behind the muscle may move with muscle contraction (animation), which is normal.
  • Breast enlargement surgery takes about one-and-a-half hours, usually under general anaesthetic; you may go home the same day but many patients spend one night in hospital.
  • You will be mobile from day one and should be back to full exercise within six weeks; one to two weeks off work is recommended.
  • At first the breasts may look high and the skin tight; this tends to settle over the first six weeks, with the long-term result emerging over 3-4 months as a more natural shape appears.
  • Scars tend to be red in the first six weeks, change to purple over the next three months, then fade to white; abnormal scarring can occur.
  • All implant shells are made of silicone; some have an additional polyurethane coating; shells are filled with silicone gel or saline, and implants have been used since the 1960s with evidence suggesting they are safe.
  • Most patients are offered silicone gel-filled implants — they feel most natural, have a range of shapes and are durable; saline implants tend to feel less natural, ripples may be more visible and they carry a risk of deflation; all other filler materials have been withdrawn for use in the UK.
  • Implants are supplied by volume and it is not possible to guarantee a cup size; the larger the implant and the slimmer the patient, the less natural the result, and an out-of-proportion implant is more likely to cause drooping, tissue stretching and palpability.
  • Implants are round or teardrop-shaped (anatomical); round implants give bigger volume at the top and are the same width as tall, while teardrop implants allow width and height to be chosen separately; both come in varying degrees of projection.
  • Texturing reduces capsular contracture (particularly with implants placed in front of the muscle) and reduces movement or rotation; anatomical implants tend to be textured because rotation would alter the shape, while rotation of a round implant is not noticeable.
  • Textured surfaces are related to BIA-ALCL, an uncommon condition; smooth-surface implants currently appear to have no link to BIA-ALCL; smooth implants are almost always round and can take several months to settle, and may slip sideways (lateral displacement) or drop below the crease (bottoming out).
  • Small quantities of silicone from implants can be taken up by the body and found in breast tissue and sometimes armpit lymph glands; silicone granuloma is inflammation and extra tissue around silicone deposits.
  • Over time the implant shell may fail and gel may leak; many ruptures are discovered by accident, and a ruptured implant should be removed — replacement at the same or a later operation is a choice.
  • There is no association between breast augmentation and breast cancer.
  • Serious complications are uncommon, occurring in less than 1 in 100 operations.
  • Bleeding (haematoma) occurs in less than 1 in 100, usually immediately but occasionally up to two weeks later; the breast becomes very swollen and tight and you return to theatre to have the blood removed — haematoma can increase the risk of later capsular contracture.
  • Infection occurs in less than 1 in 1000 cases, usually apparent over the first two or three weeks; most patients with an established infection around the implant need the implant removed, and a new implant cannot be inserted immediately — three to six months should wait for the infection to resolve.
  • Perfect symmetry is not an achievable goal; asymmetry can be of breast or nipple, size, shape and position, may appear more pronounced after surgery, and implants can settle differently in their pockets.
  • Some patients have a naturally wide cleavage that implants will not improve; with sub-muscular placement the cleavage can appear wider, and breasts and implants may fall to the sides when lying down, which is normal.
  • Stretch marks may develop, especially with larger implants, and veins may become more noticeable.
  • Breasts will sag with time because they are larger and heavier; the larger the implant, the more the breast will droop, and breasts may bottom out.
  • Implants do not interfere with the ability to breastfeed, though some evidence suggests milk production may be reduced in some women; there is no evidence of increased illness in children of women with silicone gel implants.
  • Every patient forms a scar capsule around the implant; capsular contracture — when this scar contracts and makes the implant feel firmer — is up to 1 in 10 of all augmentations, but most of those patients will not need revision surgery.
  • About 1% (1 in 100) a year need re-operation for any reason, so after 10 years about 10% will have had more surgery; capsular contracture is the most common reason and is likely to recur in 1 in 2 cases after secondary surgery.
  • Around 1 in 5 patients will have reduced nipple sensation; recovery can take up to 12 months, but 1 in 10 will have some permanent numbness.
  • It is common to be able to feel the implant, especially in slim patients or those with little breast tissue; this is an inevitable consequence of the operation and will not improve with time; lipomodelling can improve the situation in some patients.
  • The American Core study (FDA Update 2011) suggested 1 in 10 implants had ruptured at 10 years, and half of all implants may rupture by 15 years; many ruptures are silent, contained within the capsule, and do not appear harmful.
  • There is no universally agreed replacement schedule for implants and it is unusual to need exchange before ten years; if you have noticed no change you do not need regular follow-up or scans — but you should be prepared personally and financially for possible future surgery.
  • Other reasons for re-operation include wanting larger implants, shape change with time or after pregnancy and weight fluctuation, rotation of teardrop implants, and intermittent swelling around implants.
  • Long-term problems will not usually be covered by the package bought at the time of augmentation, and the NHS should not be expected to provide future private treatment.
  • BIA-ALCL is recognised by the WHO as a condition associated with breast implants; it is not a breast cancer but a cancer of the scar tissue capsule, occurring between 2 and 28 years after insertion (average 8 years), usually presenting as swelling around the implant (seroma), and usually treated by removing the implant and capsule.
  • Most BIA-ALCL cases worldwide have occurred with textured implants, with higher numbers where the texture is coarser; breast implants continue to have safety approval from the MHRA and FDA and continue to be used in reconstruction worldwide.
  • Breast Implant Illness (BII) is a term used by some patients for symptoms including tiredness, brain fog, joint aches, immune-related symptoms, sleep disturbance, depression, hormonal issues, headaches, hair loss, chills, rash and neurological issues; it is not a medical diagnosis and there is no proven association with implants.
  • Some patients report symptoms improve if implants are removed, but this is not true for all; research continues.
  • Implants do not make breast self-examination more difficult, but they do interfere with mammography because X-rays cannot pass through the implant; tell the mammography service you have implants — special views or a different centre may be used, and some patients opt for private MRI screening.
  • It is safe to sunbathe and fly with implants; implant massage is not needed and is not recommended with modern textured implants; routine implant replacement after a specified time is not recommended.
  • The only alternative surgical technique to enlarge the breast is lipofilling: fat removed by liposuction from hips, thighs or tummy and injected into the breast; only a relatively small amount can be injected so multiple operations are needed for a worthwhile effect, and some fat is absorbed in the initial weeks — fat that lasts brings permanent enlargement.
  • Your own fat is the only substance that can be safely injected into the breast; other materials have been tried and withdrawn — do not allow anyone to inject anything other than your own fat.
  • Breast uplift (mastopexy) is a different operation that lifts the nipple and breast tissue and tightens the skin without an implant; scarring is more obvious, and uplifted breasts tend to droop again with time and gravity.
  • Mild droopiness can be improved by augmentation alone, but where volume loss and droopiness both bother you, augmentation alone will not solve drooping — your surgeon should discuss augmentation with mastopexy, as one operation or in two stages.
  • In the UK the national Breast and Cosmetic Implant Registry records all implants placed or removed, allowing patients to be traced in the event of a future recall and identification of trends; entry requires consent and is strongly recommended.
  • Avoid any deal with a non-refundable deposit or financial inducement to proceed — even refunding a consultation fee if you proceed with surgery is considered an inducement and against GMC guidance.
  • A package price covering the entire process and the cost of treating complications in the initial weeks is appropriate; the cheapest deal may not be the best.
  • Before your consultation it should be possible to obtain an approximate cost from your private hospital or the surgeon's secretary; after consultation(s) you should be given a written quote.

Breast implant safety

BAAPS information on breast implant associated conditions — Breast Implant Illness (BII), BIA-ALCL, BIA-SCC, PIP implants — and the association's published safety statements.

Breast Implant Safety

Safety information page

BAAPS information and guidance on breast implant associated conditions, with links to patient documents on Breast Implant Illness (BII) and BIA-ALCL, the association's updated BII statement of October 2022, joint statements on BIA-SCC and other breast implant associated lymphomas, PRASEAG guidance, the Allergan Natrelle textured implant withdrawal statement, the BAAPS/ABS/BAPRAS joint statement on breast implant safety, and BAAPS advice on PIP implants including signs and symptoms of rupture or inflammation.

  • BAAPS publishes patient documents on Breast Implant Illness (BII) and Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (BIA-ALCL), plus an updated BII statement from October 2022.
  • In July 2023 BAAPS issued a joint statement on Breast Implant Associated Squamous Cell Carcinoma and other breast implant associated lymphomas.
  • PRASEAG issued a statement on breast implants and guidance for patients following MHRA advice on BIA-ALCL, with BAAPS, BAPRAS and the Association of Breast Surgery working together.
  • BAAPS issued statements on the withdrawal of Allergan (Natrelle) textured implants and a joint BAAPS/ABS/BAPRAS statement on breast implant safety (27 November 2018).
  • On PIP implants the 2013 expert group found no evidence they were responsible for an increased rate of breast cancer; the gel was less cohesive than most contemporary implants and had a greater potential to cause local inflammation on rupture.
  • Signs of PIP rupture, leak or inflammation include lumpiness of the breast, lumpiness or swelling of regional lymph nodes, change in shape and size, redness, tenderness, swelling and firmness; symptoms may include pain and hypersensitivity.
  • Patients unsure of their implant make should contact their surgeon or provider; patients with signs or symptoms of rupture or irritation should seek advice from their surgeon.
  • BAAPS advised removal or replacement of PIP implants as a precaution because of the inferior quality of the gel, regardless of rupture rate.
  • Breast implants continue to have safety approval from government organisations such as the UK MHRA and USA FDA and continue to be used in reconstruction worldwide.

Consumer safety guidelines

BAAPS fourteen-point consumer safety guidance for anyone considering aesthetic surgery, from making your own decision to checking credentials and taking your time.

BAAPS Consumer Safety Guidelines

Safety guidance

BAAPS fourteen-point consumer safety guidance for anyone considering aesthetic surgery: make your own decision, do your research, ask the right questions at every stage, know your surgeon and check credentials on the GMC specialist register, beware pressurising selling and non-refundable deposits, expect a two-week cooling-off period, get a second opinion if needed, time the surgery well, think about location and travel, talk to your GP, remember you can change your mind, use common sense about special offers, and take your time.

  • Only you can decide whether to go ahead with aesthetic surgery, but you need specialist input to understand what is possible, suitable and the risks and benefits.
  • No procedure is 100% risk free and no surgeon can give a 100% guarantee of results; research the limitations and risks before any consultation.
  • Know what will happen at every stage — pre-operative assessment, the day of surgery, aftercare, recovery time, follow-up and the possibility of further procedures.
  • Your consultation should be with the actual surgeon who will operate; clinic managers and nurses should not be your only point of contact.
  • A specialist plastic surgeon should have the FCRS (Plast) qualification and be listed on the Specialist Register of Plastic Surgeons with the GMC.
  • Avoid any marketing or selling technique that financially or temporally traps you, including booking fees and non-refundable advances; your decision should be free of incentive.
  • You should expect a two-week cooling-off period following your consultation to consider your options.
  • Get a second opinion if necessary; a reputable surgeon will never apply a time limit, withhold key information or upsell additional surgery.
  • Avoid surgery around major life events such as moving house, changing job, bereavement, relationship breakdown or the arrival of children.
  • Give careful consideration to travelling long distances or overseas for surgery; travel insurance often will not cover treatment or extra nights for elective aesthetic procedures.
  • Your GP can offer unbiased advice with no vested interest and may discuss functional, psychological and social benefits.
  • You can cancel right up until the time you go to sleep for surgery.
  • Don't be tempted by special offers or rushed into a quick surgery slot; anything that seems too good to be true probably is.
  • Take as much time as you need after an initial consultation; a surgeon might recommend two consultations before booking a procedure.

blocks.lead: The statements below summarise what BAAPS and the joint booklet say about breast enlargement and related decisions. The right-hand column links to the source page.
head: Topic
What BAAPS says
Source
rows: Breast augmentation (bilateral breast augmentation or BBA) is an operation to enlarge the breasts, usually by inserting an implant beneath the breast tissue; it is also commonly known as a boob job, enlargement, implant or breast size.
It can be a life-enhancing procedure, but having a breast enlargement is a big decision: it is major surgery with potential risks, and the result you may hope for cannot be guaranteed.
The joint ABS, BAAPS and BAPRAS booklet is for those looking for more information about breast augmentation, designed to be used alongside discussions with your surgeon, GP, family and friends.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Augmentation will enlarge breasts that have always been small and can fill out breasts that used to be larger, for example after pregnancy; it will reshape breasts to some extent and can correct unequal size.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Your initial consultation should be with the surgeon who will do the operation; you will be examined and measurements taken, and implant shapes, sizes and pocket positions discussed; sizers or 3D photography are only a guide because the same implant can look very different in different people.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

You should be given a cooling-off period of at least two weeks before surgery and offered a second consultation; nobody needs urgent breast augmentation, and if you are pressured to proceed you should walk away.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Breast augmentation is a lifetime commitment and must not be considered a one-stop permanent solution; you will need revision surgery as the years go by and must be prepared personally and financially.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

All surgeons should be listed on the GMC specialist register with a licence to practise; surgeons may also be registered with ABS, BAAPS and/or BAPRAS, whose members hold a standard set of recognised qualifications.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

You should avoid non-refundable deposits and financial inducements to proceed — even refunding a consultation fee if you book surgery is against GMC guidance; a written quote should follow consultation, and the cheapest deal may not be the best.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Cosmetic breast augmentation is not available on the NHS except in exceptional circumstances such as very uneven breasts, no breasts, or as part of reconstruction; after surgery abroad the NHS will only deal with emergency complications on return.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)
Implants are usually inserted through an incision under the breast at the crease, but can also be put in via an incision in the armpit or around the nipple.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Implants sit either behind the breast on top of the chest wall muscle (sub-glandular) or behind the breast and muscle (sub-muscular); dual plane combines the two; animation of sub-muscular implants with muscle contraction is normal.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Surgery takes about one-and-a-half hours under general anaesthetic; many patients spend one night in hospital, are mobile from day one, back to full exercise within six weeks, and should take one to two weeks off work.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)
Breasts may look high and tight at first, settling over six weeks with the long-term result emerging over 3-4 months; scars are red for six weeks, purple for three months, then fade to white.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

All implant shells are silicone, filled with silicone gel or saline; most patients are offered silicone gel implants for natural feel and durability; all other filler materials have been withdrawn for use in the UK.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Implants are supplied by volume and it is not possible to guarantee a cup size; larger implants on a slimmer frame look less natural and are more likely to cause complications such as drooping and tissue stretching.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Implants are round or teardrop-shaped with varying projection; texturing reduces capsular contracture and rotation, anatomical implants tend to be textured, and textured surfaces are related to BIA-ALCL while smooth implants currently appear not to be.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)
Serious complications are uncommon with breast augmentation, occurring in less than 1 in 100 operations.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Bleeding (haematoma) risk is less than 1 in 100, usually immediate but occasionally up to two weeks later; return to theatre is needed to remove the blood, and haematoma can increase the risk of later capsular contracture.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)
Infection occurs in less than 1 in 1000 cases; most established infections around an implant require removal, with three to six months before a new implant can be inserted.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)
Perfect symmetry is not an achievable goal; asymmetry can involve size, shape, nipple position and implant settling, and may appear more pronounced after surgery.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Noticeable firmness or capsular contracture occurs in up to 1 in 10 of all augmentations, but most of those patients will not need revision surgery; re-operation for any reason is about 1% a year, around 10% after 10 years, with contracture the most common reason.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)
Around 1 in 5 patients will have reduced nipple sensation; recovery can take up to 12 months, but 1 in 10 patients will have some permanent numbness.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)
It is common to be able to feel the implant, especially in slim patients or those with little breast tissue; this is an inevitable consequence of the operation and will not improve with time.

Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

BIA-ALCL is a rare cancer of the implant capsule recognised by the WHO, occurring 2 to 28 years after insertion (average 8 years), usually presenting as swelling around the implant, most often with textured implants — especially coarser textures — and usually treated by removing the implant and capsule.

Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Implants interfere with mammography because X-rays cannot pass through them; tell the screening service you have implants so special views can be taken, and the more breast volume that is implant the greater the problem; some patients choose private MRI screening.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)
Implants do not interfere with the ability to breastfeed, though some evidence suggests milk production may be reduced; pregnancy and breastfeeding may adversely affect the shape of the breast.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)
It is safe to sunbathe and fly with implants; implant massage is not needed and is not recommended with modern textured implants.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Lipofilling is the only alternative surgical technique to enlarge the breast; only a relatively small amount of fat can be injected so multiple operations are needed, some fat is absorbed early, and fat that lasts brings permanent enlargement — your own fat is the only substance that can be safely injected.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Mastopexy lifts the nipple and breast tissue and tightens skin without an implant; where both volume loss and droopiness are concerns, augmentation with mastopexy — as one operation or two stages — should be discussed.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

The UK Breast and Cosmetic Implant Registry records all implants placed or removed so patients can be traced in a future recall; entry requires consent and is strongly recommended for anyone having implant-based surgery.
Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)
Breast implants continue to have safety approval from government organisations such as the UK MHRA and USA FDA and continue to be used in breast reconstruction worldwide.
In July 2023 BAAPS issued a joint statement on Breast Implant Associated Squamous Cell Carcinoma and other breast implant associated lymphomas.

The 2013 expert group found no evidence PIP implants increased breast cancer rate, but the gel was less cohesive and had greater potential to cause local inflammation; BAAPS advised removal or replacement as a precaution.

Signs of PIP rupture, leak or inflammation include breast lumpiness, lymph node swelling, change in shape or size, redness, tenderness, swelling and firmness; symptoms may include pain and hypersensitivity.
Only you can decide whether to go ahead with aesthetic surgery; no procedure is 100% risk free and no surgeon can give a 100% guarantee of results.
You should expect a two-week cooling-off period following your consultation, and should avoid booking fees, non-refundable advances and any technique that traps you into proceeding.
Your consultation should be with the surgeon who will operate, and a specialist plastic surgeon should have FCRS (Plast) and be on the GMC Specialist Register of Plastic Surgeons.

Avoid surgery around major life events, consider travel and insurance implications carefully, talk to your GP, and take as much time as you need — you can cancel up until the time you go to sleep for surgery.

BAAPS patient information describes practice in the United Kingdom; costs, funding, professional registration and clinical standards differ between countries, and local standards still apply where a procedure is performed. Cosmetic breast augmentation is generally private in the UK; the NHS may fund it only in exceptional circumstances.

The joint booklet Your Guide to Breast Augmentation is published by the Association of Breast Surgery, BAAPS and BAPRAS (Edition 2, BAPRAS London, 2021; editors Lee Martin and Emma de Sousa; reviewed by PRASEAG). This library stores only summaries, extracted facts and links to publicly available BAAPS pages and PDFs; BAAPS content remains the property of BAAPS and the respective publishing bodies.

For US regulator guidance, see the FDA information library. For UK health-service guidance, see the NHS information library. For academic patient education, see the Cleveland Clinic information library. For published research, see the PMC research library.

blocks.html:
All sections of the review

Grouped by theme. Each entry gives a short summary, the main extracted points and a direct link to that section of the NCBI Bookshelf article.

Background and anatomy

What breast augmentation is, why it is performed, how the FDA has treated silicone implants over time, and the anatomy the operation works on. (3)

Continuing Education Activity

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

The review's opening summary: breast augmentation increases breast size, most often with an implant and less commonly with fat transfer, and is among the most commonly performed plastic surgery procedures in the United States. It frames the activity around indications, contraindications, complications and the role of the interprofessional team before and after surgery.

  • Objectives are to identify the different techniques, describe the indications, review the complications and improve care coordination among the team.
  • The FDA restricted silicone-filled implants for cosmetic enhancement from 1992; reconstructive patients continued to receive them after mastectomy.
  • The activity is written for the interprofessional team involved in pre- and postoperative care.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Introduction

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Breast augmentation is a surgical procedure in which breast size is enhanced, either by placing an implant or, less commonly, through fat transfer. The section traces FDA policy on silicone implants from the 1992 restriction to the 2006 reversal, describes the shift towards cohesive gel and form-stable implants, and sets out monitoring advice and the fact that implants are not permanent devices.

  • Extensive research failed to confirm the disease fears that led to the 1992 silicone restriction, and the FDA allowed general use of silicone-filled implants again in 2006.
  • By 2017 the majority of patients undergoing augmentation received cohesive gel silicone implants, with makers introducing different levels of gel firmness.
  • The FDA recommends MRI screening every two years in patients with silicone implants to detect subclinical leaks, but adherence is incomplete and MRI readings can be false positive.
  • Higher gel cohesion may lower rupture rates, but the review states that eventually all implants will rupture or break.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Anatomy and Physiology

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

The anatomy relevant to augmentation: the breast sits on the anterior chest wall below the clavicle, bounded medially by the sternum, laterally by the latissimus dorsi and inferiorly by the inframammary fold, with the pectoralis muscles forming its posterior boundary.

  • The inframammary fold is a dermal structure formed by fusion of the superficial and mammary fascia.
  • Blood supply comes from the subdermal plexus with major contributions from the internal mammary artery, external mammary artery and intercostal perforators.
  • Nerve supply is mainly through the intercostal plexus, with most contribution from the third to fifth intercostal nerves.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Indications and contraindications

Who the review says the procedure is for, and the conditions that should stop a surgeon from operating. (2)

Indications

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Implants are placed for reconstruction after mastectomy, for developmental disorders such as hypomastia, and for elective reasons related to self-image. Hypomastia may follow normal development or involution, especially after pregnancy, and people of all personality types may seek the procedure.

  • Reported motivations include reconstruction, developmental under-development of the breast and elective enhancement of self-image.
  • The review notes that when surveyed after surgery, the vast majority of women would undergo the operation again.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Contraindications

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Most patients have no contraindications, but the review lists the conditions that should prevent surgery and the patient factors that should pause it.

  • Absolute reasons not to operate include active infection of the breast, active cancer and pregnancy.
  • Relative reasons include a history of autoimmune disease, current radiation treatment, unstable medical conditions and known sensitivity to silicone.
  • Psychological instability or unrealistic expectations are also given as reasons not to proceed.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

The operation

Equipment, theatre team, preparation, implant choices, placement, incisions, anaesthesia, duration and expected recovery. (4)

Equipment

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Routine operating-room equipment is usually sufficient. Extras depend on the approach: a lighted retractor or headlight for visualising the pocket, an endoscope for umbilical or axillary approaches, and sometimes an implant sleeve used as part of a no-touch technique.

  • A no-touch technique limits handling of the implant to reduce implant trauma and bacterial contamination.
  • Endoscopic equipment may be required when the umbilical or axillary route is used.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Personnel

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

The operating team normally consists of the surgeon, a scrubbed assistant, an anaesthesiologist and a circulating nurse working together in the operating room.

  • Standard theatre roles apply: surgeon, scrubbed assistant, anaesthesiologist and circulating nurse.
  • The team structure is described as the same as for other routine surgical procedures.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Preparation

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Patients are prepared for surgery as for any other surgical procedure, following the usual preoperative pathway.

  • Preparation follows the routine preoperative work-up used for any operation, including assessment and consent.
  • The review places emphasis on informed consent and on the pre-operative teaching that reduces later problems.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Technique or Treatment

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Two main implant types are described, saline-filled and silicone-filled, both with a silicone outer shell that can be smooth or textured. Implants can sit above or beneath the pectoralis muscle, be reached through inframammary, transaxillary or peri-areolar incisions, and are usually done as an outpatient operation under general anaesthesia.

  • Saline implants are inserted empty and filled through a port, typically with a 25 to 50 mL range specified by the manufacturer.
  • Saline implants are FDA-approved from age 18 for augmentation and at any age for reconstruction; silicone gel implants are approved from age 22.
  • Silicone implants suit patients with thin soft-tissue coverage better, showing less rippling and a softer, more natural feel.
  • Texturing prevents rotation in shaped implants and may lower capsular contracture in the subglandular pocket, but not in the submuscular pocket.
  • No single placement method is uniformly accepted as best; the choice is made jointly by patient and surgeon.
  • The operation generally takes 45 to 90 minutes; most patients return to light work within a week, with full activity taking up to six weeks.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Complications and outcomes

Early and late complications, capsular contracture, implant longevity, reported satisfaction and how the care team reduces risk. (4)

Complications

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Complication rates are described as low, but no implant is a lifetime device. Early problems include infection, bleeding and sensory change; later problems include malposition, deflation or leak and capsular contracture, which may require further surgery.

  • Surgeons commonly estimate a 15 to 20 year lifespan for implants, with no uniform recommendation on routine replacement.
  • Early complications listed are infection, scarring, asymmetry, haematoma, seroma, breast pain, poor cosmetic outcome and changes in nipple or breast sensation.
  • Later complications listed are implant malposition or displacement, implant deflation or leak, and capsular contracture.
  • Capsular contracture is graded 1 to 4 and may require surgical correction or implant removal when severe.
  • Staphylococcus epidermidis and Cutibacterium acnes are the microorganisms most commonly isolated in studies of capsular contracture, supporting a suspected biofilm or low-grade infection mechanism.
  • A slim possibility of breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) is reported, possibly linked to a particular type of implant texturing, although the exact relationship is not yet determined.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Clinical Significance

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

The procedure remains highly popular, and the review stresses that clinicians treating women with implants should be aware of them, because the implants are relevant to other conditions and to screening.

  • The American Society of Plastic Surgeons reported approximately 290,000 augmentation procedures performed in the United States in 2016.
  • The vast majority of patients report improved self-esteem and satisfaction with the decision.
  • Doctors treating these patients for other conditions should have an awareness of the procedure and of implants in general.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Risk reduction is described as a team effort: informed consent, nurse-led preoperative instruction, smoking cessation, pharmacist medicines checks and early recognition of problems. Outcomes are reported as good, with most patients pleased with the result.

  • Many past litigations arose primarily from a lack of informed consent, which the pre-operative visit is meant to address.
  • Patients should be instructed to stop smoking and make positive lifestyle changes so results last longer.
  • Pharmacists contribute by checking allergies and explaining medicines, which can reduce infection and help pain control.
  • Surveys cited in the review indicate about 70 to 80 percent of patients are satisfied and feel the outcome was perfect.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

References and Further Reading

StatPearls reference list · Last updated 2023-07-18

The review cites twelve sources spanning secondary augmentation, transgender breast contouring, anatomical versus round implants, fat grafting, capsular contracture risk factors, cosmetic-tourism infection, subclinical implant infection, outcomes series and long-term follow-up.

  • The full reference list, with links to each PubMed record, is reproduced in the references section of this page.
  • Every citation can be checked at source through its PMID link.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

blocks.lead: The statements below summarise what the StatPearls review says about breast augmentation. The right-hand column links to the section each statement came from.
head: Topic
What the review says
Source section
rows: Breast augmentation is a surgical procedure in which breast size is enhanced, either by placing an implant or, less commonly, through fat transfer.

The review describes augmentation as one of the most commonly performed plastic surgery procedures in the United States, and the American Society of Plastic Surgeons reported about 290,000 procedures in 2016.
The FDA restricted silicone-filled implants for cosmetic enhancement from 1992, and allowed them again without clinical-study enrolment in 2006 after studies failed to confirm disease links.

The FDA recommends MRI screening every two years for patients with silicone implants to detect subclinical leaks, but the review notes that patients and physicians do not always follow this and that MRI can be falsely positive.
No implant is a lifetime device: surgeons commonly estimate a 15 to 20 year lifespan, and there is no uniform recommendation on routine replacement at a set interval.
Current implants use more cohesive, or 'gummy', gel than earlier generations, which may lower rupture rates, but the review states that all implants will eventually rupture or break.

The breast sits on the anterior chest wall below the clavicle, bounded medially by the sternum, laterally by the latissimus dorsi and inferiorly by the inframammary fold, with the pectoralis major and minor behind it.

Blood supply comes from the subdermal plexus with contributions from the internal mammary, external mammary and intercostal perforators; sensation is mainly from the third to fifth intercostal nerves.
Indications include reconstruction after mastectomy, developmental disorders such as hypomastia, including involution after pregnancy, and elective enhancement of self-image.

The review states that the vast majority of women surveyed after surgery would undergo the operation again, and surveys cited indicate about 70 to 80 percent of patients are satisfied with the outcome.
Active breast infection, active cancer and pregnancy rule out surgery; autoimmune disease history, current radiotherapy, unstable medical conditions and known silicone sensitivity are also listed.
Psychological instability or unrealistic expectations are given as reasons not to operate, alongside the medical contraindications.
Saline implants are inserted empty and inflated through a port, usually with a 25 to 50 mL fill range set by the manufacturer, and are FDA-approved from age 18 for augmentation.
Silicone gel implants are FDA-approved for patients aged 22 and over, though surgeons may use them off-label below 22, and they suit thin patients with little soft-tissue coverage better.
Textured shells help prevent rotation of shaped implants and may lower capsular contracture when the implant is placed in the subglandular pocket, but not in the submuscular pocket.
Implants can be placed above the muscle (subglandular) or beneath it (submuscular); no single placement is accepted as uniformly best and the choice is made jointly with the surgeon.
Common access incisions are the inframammary crease, the transaxillary route and the peri-areolar route.
General anaesthesia is most common, although sedation or local anaesthesia can be used in selected cases, and the operation is an outpatient procedure taking 45 to 90 minutes.
Recovery is usually rapid, with a return to light work and activity within a week and a return to full activity that may take up to six weeks.
The operating team normally consists of the surgeon, a scrubbed assistant, an anaesthesiologist and a circulating nurse.
An implant sleeve may be used as part of a no-touch technique that minimises handling of the implant, to reduce implant trauma and bacterial contamination.
Early postoperative complications listed are infection, scarring, asymmetry, haematoma, seroma, breast pain, poor cosmetic outcome and changes in nipple or breast sensation.
Later complications listed are implant malposition or displacement, implant deflation or leak, and capsular contracture, which is tightening of the tissue capsule around the implant.

Capsular contracture is graded 1 to 4 and may need surgical correction or implant removal; a low-grade infection or biofilm is suspected as a cause, with Staphylococcus epidermidis and Cutibacterium acnes most commonly isolated.

The review reports a slim possibility that women with breast implants are more likely to be diagnosed with anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), possibly associated with a certain type of texturing, although the exact relationship has not been determined.

Nurse-led preoperative instruction, stopping smoking, pharmacist allergy and medicines checks, and interprofessional follow-up are described as ways to lower complication rates, with earlier recognition improving outcomes.

MedlinePlus is a consumer-health information service of the U.S. National Library of Medicine. It does not provide medical advice, endorse any clinic, surgeon or treatment package, or approve breast enlargement as a procedure. Nothing here is a recommendation to have a treatment, and individual suitability can only be assessed in a consultation.

Summaries and key points are condensed from MedlinePlus pages for readability. They are not a substitute for the original documents, which may have been updated since this library was compiled on 2026-10-20. Always read the current version on medlineplus.gov and discuss it with a qualified clinician.

blocks.html:
All MedlinePlus pages in this library

Grouped by topic. Each entry gives a short summary, the main extracted points and a direct link to the full MedlinePlus page.

Breast augmentation surgery

The MedlinePlus encyclopedia article on the operation itself: what it is, how implants are placed, the anaesthetic and incision options, why it is performed, and the full risk list.

Breast augmentation surgery

Medical Encyclopedia article · Page last reviewed 2025-02-17

The MedlinePlus overview of breast augmentation: enlarging or reshaping the breasts by placing an implant behind the breast tissue or under the chest muscle fascia. The article covers the two implant fills (sterile saline and silicone), the outpatient or hospital setting, general versus local anaesthetic, the four usual incision routes, how implant and technique choices affect pain, appearance, implant integrity and future mammograms, the reasons for surgery, the risks (including capsular contracture, implant rupture, breast implant-associated lymphoma and reported systemic symptoms), what to arrange before the operation, what happens afterwards, and the expected outcome.

  • Augmentation is done by placing an implant behind the breast tissue or beneath the chest muscle, and implants are sacs filled with either sterile salt water or silicone.
  • The operation is performed at an outpatient surgery clinic or in a hospital, most often under general anaesthetic, with local anaesthetic as an alternative.
  • Four incision routes are described: the natural fold under the breast (the most common), the armpit using an endoscope, the edge of the areola, and, for saline implants only, a route near the navel through which the empty implant is tunnelled and then filled.
  • An areola-edge incision may bring more difficulty with breastfeeding and more loss of nipple sensation, and may carry a higher risk of capsular contracture.
  • Implant type, implant size and the chosen operation influence post-operative pain, the appearance achieved, the chance of later breakage or leakage, and the extra views future mammograms will need.
  • Reasons for the procedure include increasing breast size, changing breast shape and correcting a congenital deformity; patients are told to expect improvement rather than perfection.
  • Risks shared with any operation are listed as reactions to medicines, breathing problems, bleeding, blood clots and infection.
  • Breast-specific risks include difficulty breastfeeding, numbness around the nipple or surrounding skin, small or thickened raised scars, uneven nipple position, differences in size or shape between the two breasts, implant breakage or leakage, visible rippling, infection requiring implant removal, the need for more breast surgery and puncture of the lung.
  • A capsule of scar tissue normally forms around a new implant; when it thickens it can change the breast's shape, harden the breast tissue or cause pain.
  • A rare immune-system cancer, breast implant-associated lymphoma, has been reported with some implants, presenting as a mass or swelling around the implant with breast pain and treated by removing the implant and the tissue around it.
  • Some people report systemic symptoms after implants — grouped under breast implant illness, which the page says is not yet established as a recognised illness — including fatigue, memory and concentration problems, joint and muscle pain, anxiety, hair loss, depression, rash, autoimmune disease, inflammation and weight change; some improve after removal and some do not.
  • Before surgery patients should ask about a screening mammogram, disclose any pregnancy possibility and every medicine or supplement they take, review diabetes, heart disease and other conditions, stop smoking (which slows healing and raises clot risk), prepare the home and arrange transport and help for one to two days.
  • During the week before surgery, blood thinners such as aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen and vitamin E are commonly paused on the surgeon's advice, and fasting and morning-medicine instructions come from the surgical team.
  • Afterwards the breasts are wrapped in bulky gauze or a surgical bra, drainage tubes are removed within about three days, and massaging from around day five may be suggested to reduce capsular hardening after checking with the provider.
  • Outcomes are usually very good, scars are permanent and most visible during the first year before fading, a supportive bra may be worn for a few months, and later tests may be advised to confirm the implants are intact.

Read the original on medlineplus.gov →

Recovery, discharge and wound care

Patient instructions for the days and weeks after cosmetic breast surgery, plus general guidance for looking after a surgical incision that has been left open.

Cosmetic breast surgery - discharge

Patient instructions · Page last reviewed 2025-02-17

Home-care instructions after cosmetic breast surgery — augmentation, lift or reduction. It covers what happens in hospital, what to expect once home, activity and driving limits, dressing and wound care, pain medicines and general self-care, and the symptoms that should prompt a call to the surgical team.

  • Surgery is done under general or local anaesthetic and takes an hour or more; patients wake with a gauze dressing or surgical bra and may have drainage tubes in place.
  • Most people go home the same day, though some stay one to two nights in hospital.
  • Pain, bruising and swelling are normal and settle over days to weeks, and reduced sensation in the breast skin or nipple may return gradually.
  • Short walks are encouraged early to support circulation; returning to work or other activities commonly takes 7 to 14 days or longer.
  • Heavy lifting, strenuous exercise and overstretching the arms are avoided for 3 to 6 weeks, and driving should wait at least two weeks and until drowsiness-inducing pain medicines have stopped.
  • Drainage tubes are removed at a visit within a few days and stitches within two weeks; surgical glue dissolves on its own and does not need removing.
  • Dressings stay in place as instructed, incisions are kept clean, dry and covered, and are checked daily for redness, pain or drainage.
  • Once dressings are no longer needed, a soft wireless supportive bra is worn day and night for 2 to 4 weeks; bathing is limited to showering after drains come out, with baths, hot tubs and swimming deferred until stitches and drains are out and the surgeon agrees.
  • Scars may take several months to more than a year to fade, and sunblock of SPF 30 or higher is advised whenever the scars are exposed.
  • Smoking is not permitted because it slows healing and raises the risk of complications and infection; alcohol is avoided while taking narcotic pain medicines, and aspirin, ibuprofen and other medicines or supplements need the surgeon's approval.
  • The surgeon should be contacted for increasing pain, redness, swelling, yellow or green drainage, bleeding or bruising at the incision, medicine side effects, a temperature of 100°F (38°C) or higher, numbness, loss of motion, or sudden swelling of the breast.

Read the original on medlineplus.gov →

Surgical wound care - open

Patient instructions · Page last reviewed 2026-01-01

General MedlinePlus instructions for looking after a surgical incision that has broken open and is being left to heal rather than re-closed with stitches. It explains healing from the inside out, hand hygiene before dressing changes, removing and replacing dressings, cleaning and irrigating the wound, disposal of used supplies, and the signs that mean a call to the provider. The breast augmentation article links this page for wound care after breast surgery.

  • A wound left open heals from the inside out, and the dressing absorbs drainage so the surface skin does not close before the tissue underneath has filled in.
  • Hands should be washed before every dressing change — an alcohol cleanser, or soap and water for 15 to 30 seconds including under the nails, with jewellery removed.
  • The skin around the wound is cleaned with saline or mild soapy water; alcohol, peroxide, iodine and antibacterial cleansers are avoided because they can damage wound tissue and slow healing.
  • Where irrigation is advised, a syringe of saline or soapy water is held about 2.5 to 15 cm from the wound to wash away discharge, then the area is patted dry.
  • No lotion, cream or herbal remedy goes on or near the wound without the provider's agreement; dressings are used once only and soiled material is bagged before disposal.
  • Contact the provider for more redness, pain, swelling or bleeding, a wound that looks larger, deeper, dried out or dark, thicker or foul-smelling discharge, or a temperature of 100.5°F (38°C) or higher.

Read the original on medlineplus.gov →

Health topic page · Page last reviewed 2024-12-17

The MedlinePlus health topic hub for plastic and cosmetic surgery. It summarises the body areas people most often have reshaped — including increasing, reducing or reshaping sagging breasts — and links out to the encyclopedia articles and image series, the breast lift video, ASPS plastic surgery statistics, ClinicalTrials.gov searches for breast implants and plastic surgery, and patient handouts including the breast augmentation article in this library.

  • Breast surgery appears among the most commonly requested cosmetic changes: enlarging, reducing or reshaping sagging breasts.
  • The page indexes the breast augmentation, lift and reduction encyclopedia articles, their image series and the breast lift anatomy video.
  • It links to FDA breast implant information, American Society of Plastic Surgeons statistics and ClinicalTrials.gov searches for breast implants and plastic surgery procedures.

blocks.heading: Key facts from the MedlinePlus pages
blocks.lead: The statements below summarise what MedlinePlus says about breast enlargement and the decisions around it. The right-hand column links to the source page.
head: Topic
What MedlinePlus says
Source
rows: MedlinePlus describes breast augmentation as a procedure to enlarge the breasts or change their shape, carried out by placing an implant behind the breast tissue or under the muscle fascia or chest muscle.
An implant is a sac filled with either sterile salt water (saline) or a material called silicone.

The operation is done at an outpatient surgery clinic or in a hospital, with most women receiving general anaesthesia while local anaesthesia — staying awake with the breast area numbed — is an alternative.

Four approaches are described: a cut in the natural fold under the breast (the most common technique), a cut under the arm often using an endoscope (leaving no scar on the breast but possibly one under the arm), a cut around the areola edge, and, for saline implants, a cut near the navel through which the implant is moved up and filled.
The periareolar route may bring more problems with breastfeeding and loss of sensation around the nipple, and may carry a higher risk of capsular contracture.

The type of implant, its size and the type of surgery affect post-operative pain, the appearance of the breast, the risk of the implant breaking or leaking later, and the additional views future mammograms will require.

The procedure is carried out to increase breast size, to change breast shape, or to correct a congenital deformity, with patients advised to discuss realistic expectations — improvement rather than perfection.
Risks applying to anaesthesia and surgery in general include reactions to medicines, breathing problems, bleeding, blood clots and infection.

Listed breast risks include difficulty breastfeeding, loss of feeling in the nipple area or surrounding skin, small or thickened raised scars, uneven nipple position, differences in size or shape between the breasts, breaking or leakage of the implant, visible rippling, removal of the implant because of infection, the need for further breast surgery and puncture of the lung.
A capsule of scar tissue normally forms around a new implant to hold it in place; if this capsule thickens and grows it can change the breast's shape, harden breast tissue or cause pain.

A rare lymphoma of the immune system has been reported with some implant types, presenting as a mass or swelling around the implant together with breast pain, and treated by removing the implant and the tissue around it; research into other cancer links is ongoing.

Some people report systemic symptoms after receiving implants — fatigue, memory and concentration problems, joint and muscle pain, anxiety, hair loss, depression, rash, autoimmune disease, inflammation and weight gain or loss — described as breast implant illness, which the page says does not yet have enough evidence to be a recognised illness; some report improvement after implant removal and others do not.
Despite these rare risks, MedlinePlus states that breast implants are considered safe.

Patients are advised to ask whether a screening mammogram is needed given their age and breast cancer risk, arranged early enough that any further imaging or biopsy cannot delay the planned operation.
The surgeon or nurse should be told about any pregnancy or possibility of pregnancy and about every medicine, drug, supplement or herb being taken, including items bought without a prescription.

Diabetes, heart disease and other conditions may require review by the provider who treats them, and smoking should be cut down or stopped because it slows healing and raises the risk of blood clots — surgery may be postponed while smoking continues.

During the week before surgery, medicines that stop blood clotting — including over-the-counter aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen and vitamin E as well as many prescription medicines — are commonly stopped temporarily on the surgeon's advice, with instructions on which medicines to still take on the day of surgery.

On the day of surgery patients follow the rules given about when to stop eating and drinking, take only the prescribed medicines with a small sip of water, and arrive at the hospital at the requested time.

Most patients go home once the anaesthetic has worn off and they can walk, drink water and use the bathroom safely; the breasts are wrapped in a bulky gauze dressing or a surgical bra, and drainage tubes, if placed, are removed within 3 days.
Massaging the breasts from about 5 days after surgery may be recommended to reduce hardening of the capsule around the implant, but should only begin after checking with the provider.

Outcomes from breast surgery are usually very good, pain and skin symptoms from the surgery generally settle, a special supportive bra may be worn for a few months, scars are permanent but typically fade after being most visible in the first year, and future tests may be recommended to confirm the implants have not ruptured.

Home instructions after cosmetic breast surgery allow short walks early, put return to work or other activity at 7 to 14 days or longer, and prohibit heavy lifting, strenuous exercise and overstretching the arms for 3 to 6 weeks, with driving delayed at least 2 weeks.

The surgical team should be contacted for increasing pain, redness, swelling, yellow or green drainage, bleeding or bruising at the incision, medicine side effects, a fever of 100°F (38°C) or higher, numbness or loss of motion, or sudden swelling of the breast.
Incision scars may take several months to more than a year to fade, and protecting them with sunblock of SPF 30 or higher is advised whenever they are exposed to the sun.

Where an incision has broken open and is not re-closed, healing proceeds from the inside out and a dressing absorbs drainage so the surface does not close over before the wound underneath has filled in.

Saline or mild soapy water is used to clean around the wound, while skin cleansers, alcohol, peroxide, iodine and antibacterial soaps are avoided because they can damage wound tissue and slow healing.

A provider should be contacted if redness, pain, swelling or bleeding increases, the wound looks larger, deeper, dried out or dark, discharge becomes thicker or smells of pus, or temperature reaches 100.5°F (38°C).

The MedlinePlus Plastic and Cosmetic Surgery topic page lists increasing, reducing and reshaping sagging breasts among the most common cosmetic requests and indexes the breast augmentation, lift and reduction articles, image series and video.

blocks.html:
The article in brief

Breast enlargement is the enlargement of the breasts. It may occur naturally as in mammoplasia or may occur artificially through active intervention. Many women regard their breasts, which are female secondary sex characteristics, as important to their sexual attractiveness, as a sign of femininity that is important to their sense of self. Due to this, when a woman considers her breasts deficient in some respect, she might choose to engage in some activity intended to enhance them.

Mammoplasia. The article names natural breast enlargement as mammoplasia, distinguishing it from enlargement produced by active intervention.

blocks.heading: Methods the article lists to achieve larger breasts
blocks.lead: The four actual and potential methods named in the article, with the wording condensed from the source. The right-hand column points to the article’s own references.
head: Method
Category
What the article says
Refs
rows: The article lists surgical breast augmentation as an actual and potential method to achieve larger breasts, naming two routes: breast implants and fat transfer (fat grafting). It links to the breast augmentation and breast implant articles for the operative detail, cost and risk information held there.

The article lists pharmacological or hormonal breast enhancement through administration of medications such as estrogen or breast enlargement supplements. Three of the article's seven citations support this method: two clinical texts on hormone therapy and breast cancer metastasis, and a 1998 study on hormonal breast augmentation and insulin-like growth factor-I (IGF-I).

The article states that by increasing food energy intake, more adipose tissue will be created, part of which will consist of adipose tissue located near the breast area. The amount added to the breasts varies from person to person and is controlled by the KLF14 gene. The article notes that additional modification of the KLF14 gene can thus make sure even more of the adipose tissue increase will occur at the breasts.

The article lists mechanical breast enhancement as a potential method, supported by a single citation: a 2007 Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery study evaluating the Brava external tissue expander and asking whether breast enlargement without surgery is a reality.

What the article says
rows: Repairing chest and breast tissue damaged by breast cancer, blunt or penetrating trauma or blast injury, and correcting developmental defects of the chest such as tuberous breast deformity.
